### TravelGuard24
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/travelguard-d181) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://travelguard24.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> policy-gated travel agent

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Webauthn](https://img.shields.io/badge/Webauthn-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vitest](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vitest-333333?style=flat-square) ![prava](https://img.shields.io/badge/prava-333333?style=flat-square) ![visa](https://img.shields.io/badge/visa-333333?style=flat-square) ![senso](https://img.shields.io/badge/senso-333333?style=flat-square) ![Duffel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Duffel-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Four hurdles that changed the code or the architecture, not just the schedule.

**A payment token from one sandbox is rejected by every other sandbox.**

The original plan was to pay the airline directly with the Prava credential. Duffel's card vault returned `403 unavailable_feature`, and their payment endpoint returned `422` demanding a `card_id` that only the endpoint that 403s can create. The alternative branch, a 3DS session, also requires that same `card_id` — a closed loop, not a missing permission.

There was a trap inside the trap. With the documented singular `data.payment` object, a card payment returns a wall of `validation_required` errors on `card_number`, `card_exp` and friends, which reads as *"Duffel does accept raw card fields and I named them wrong."* It does not. Only the array form `data.payments[]` surfaces the real `one_of` error. That cost two wasted attempts.

Prava confirmed in writing that a sandbox token is rejected at final checkout by design. So I stopped hunting for a more permissive sandbox and made the acquiring step a disclosed simulation that actually enforces the mandate — it rejects a wrong amount, a wrong merchant and a reused credential — instead of just marking the booking paid. Settlement to the airline runs over Duffel's `balance` rail, and only fires if Prava succeeded first.

**Two hours lost 

Payments started failing with `FETCH_AGENTIC_CREDS_ERROR: Visa 400 — fetching cryptogram failed`, an hour after four clean transactions on the same card.Tried various checks.Went thru latest commits to see if something broke a working flow specially when Prava said its working for them.

I saw someone posted a list of sandbox cards on Discord and I was using the first in the list which I thought most must be using.So I picked a card from middle of the lot and voila - it worked.Enrolling one fixed it instantly. Still dont know what the issue was with the first card but thats an issue perhaps for Visa or Prava to solve.

**An error that pointed at my request when the fault was in the data.**

The first end-to-end run failed with `422 invalid_order_create_type` — "the specified type was incorrect" — so I went looking for a malformed body. There wasn't one. Some airlines simply refuse to hold a seat without payment, and nothing in the offer says which: Iberia refused three times in a row while British Airways and American were fine. I couldn't bulk test either, because booking one offer makes the rest of that search return `offer_request_already_booked`.

The fix was to stop treating the cheapest compliant fare as the only candidate. The agent now walks down the list of fares that passed policy until an airline accepts, and records which ones refused. Falling back never weakens the decision, because every candidate had already passed policy.

The rejection branch - what happens when the guardrail catches a bad credential  was type checked and unit tested but had never executed against the real vendor. The first real run found two bugs. A small one: I sent `CANCELLED` and their enum is `CANCELED`, one L, which only that branch ever reaches.

And a bad one underneath it. I wrote the audit entry *after* the call to the vendor, so when that call threw on the spelling, the refusal vanished which meant no log entry, no message to the traveller, just a stack trace, with the credential still live on an open session. A system whose entire claim is that refusals are recorded lost a refusal because someone else's API didn't like my spelling. The entry is now written before any network call, with a `REPORT_FAILED` entry if reporting then fails, and a regression test pins both.

Few smaller issues: Dictating one sentence to Siri produced three different transcriptions. My date parser read `26` out of `2026` as a day of the month and put a wrong date on screen — in the exact step whose purpose is letting the traveller catch a misread. And Prava accepts the same payment report twice, so replay protection genuinely had to be mine.

**The problem it solves**

Anyone who has worked at a large corporate knows when it comes to travel booking there is the familiar path.Call the travel desk(most have Amex GBT) and start your process.Fill out forms.Talk to the agent back and forth and finally we get what the policy approved for individual.

TravelGuard24 is your corporate booking agent assigned to you at onboarding stage if your role demands frequent airline travel.

What is  TravelGuard24.Why 24 because its available 24x7 to you.

**An agent that books real flights — and refuses to book the ones it shouldn't.**

Most agentic-commerce demos answer *"can an agent complete a purchase?"* That question is largely settled. TravelGuard24 answers the one that decides whether any of this is deployable inside a large corporate : **should this purchase happen at all, and can you prove afterwards why it did or didn't?**

A traveller sends an iMessage - typed or via voice like SIRI. The agent searches live airline inventory, evaluates every fare against a corporate travel policy, and then either books it — with a payment credential network-locked to that exact fare — or blocks it, names the rule that failed, and writes a tamper-evident audit entry either way.

The blocked path is not the error case. It is the product.

Each employee gets a policy attached.It may well be a group policy.

Booking done in seconds as approval are already in policy.No more lengthy emails sharing quotes and then final confirmation.

One message, passkey based approval and off you fly...

---

### Update — the payment layer was since ported to Stripe Shared Payment Tokens

This submission is the original **Prava + Visa passkey** build, and the code behind it is private. The policy engine, Duffel integration, orchestration and audit trail were afterwards carried across to a different settlement rail, where the spend limit lives **inside the token itself** rather than in a mandate alongside it — so a rule that is a financial limit becomes `usage_limits` enforced by Stripe and the card network, and a rule that is not (cabin, carrier, advance purchase) is enforced by never minting a token at all.

That port is public, including the SPT wire shapes that are not in the documentation:

- **Source:** https://github.com/hkarekar403/TG24-Stripe-Shared-payment-tokens
- **Live demo:** https://travelguard24-stripe.vercel.app/

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

The agent uses Prava end to end: a real session, a real network token and dynamic CVV, a real WebAuthn passkey, `report-status`, and a real e-ticket issued afterwards.

The part worth judging is *where* the check happens. Visa's third pillar is about keeping payment aligned with what the user actually authorised. We run the company's travel policy **before** a mandate exists, so the credential is only ever created for a fare that already passed — and the mandate is locked to that fare's exact price, never to the budget cap. Sending the cap would mint a credential spendable above what was approved, which is weaker than a normal checkout.

The fourth pillar is the audit log: every attempt is recorded, including refusals, chained by SHA-256. To be precise about what that proves — ordering and integrity, not authorship. Signing is the next step.

Pillar 2 is visible rather than claimed. The passkey step runs on `sandbox.auth.visa.com`, which you can see in the address bar in our screenshots and video. Enrolment hits `payment-credential-binding`; repeat purchases hit `-authentication` only, which is what makes "one tap, zero typing" checkable.

This does not duplicate Prava's own guardrails. Theirs constrain a mandate that already exists — how much, where, how often. Ours decides whether the purchase should happen at all and which of 335 live fares to pick. The gate decides which purchase should exist; the mandate then network-locks that purchase.

One demo run proves the claim most spend-control tools can't make: the traveller asserted "finance approved AU$10,000" and the gate refused against the company's 1,300 cap.

**Most Startup-Ready Product**

Straight answer on two of the stated criteria: **no customers and no revenue.** This was built over a weekend and has never been sold.

What is not hypothetical is the model. Travel management companies already charge corporates a fee per booking as merchant of record, and already employ people to enforce exactly the four rules our gate checks. We are not inventing demand or a pricing model, we are removing the manual step. Prava's own order record classified our transaction as MCC 4722, "Travel Agency" — unprompted confirmation that the framing is the real one.

**Product readiness** is the axis we can actually evidence: 174 automated tests, zero runtime dependencies, a 30-case manual test plan someone with no prior knowledge can follow, and a compliance section in the README that states its own gaps rather than hiding them. That includes the two things which currently disqualify our audit log for a real SOC 1 report — it is in memory, and a hash chain proves ordering, not authorship. A product claiming to make spending auditable should be audited about itself first.

**The pitch in one line:** everyone else is solving how to complete a purchase, and finance teams have the opposite problem — purchases complete far too easily. The buyer is not the traveller, it is the CFO who needs to know a booking cannot exceed policy and that a refusal is on record.

On virality I would rather not oversell. Compliance software spreads through procurement, not word of mouth. The one thing that compounds is the policy corpus: every company onboarded adds a real policy document.

**iMessage Agent**

The whole product is triggered and approved from iMessage using Linq. You dictate a request to Siri, the agent replies in the same thread, and if the fare passes policy it sends back an approval link that opens in Safari where Face ID satisfies the passkey. You never leave Messages and there is no app. Measured 41 seconds from message to issued e-ticket.

We poll Linq rather than use webhooks, so nothing connects inward and the whole system runs on localhost with no tunnel.

Two things that cost me time and might save someone else's:

- **Envelope asymmetry.** Message parts arrive top-level when you read them, but have to be nested under `message` when you send. Sending the read shape returns `1005 at least one message part is required`, which reads like a malformed part when the part is fine.
- **Anchor the poll to process start and dedupe on message id.** Otherwise restarting the server books a flight off an old message, and every subsequent tick re-books it.

One design decision came out of using it: we deleted the confirm-on-laptop step. Searching and checking policy spend nothing, so there is nothing to ask permission for — the only human action left is the passkey, on the phone. The laptop became a compliance console instead of an approval surface.

**Agent Commerce Discovery & Trust**

Senso decides which airlines the agent may transact with at all, so it sits directly in front of a spending decision rather than being a recommendation shown after one.

The problem it fixes is provenance. Our `policy.json` restates rules that really live in a signed company document, and that restatement is not evidence — the audit entry would be citing something a developer typed rather than the clause a CFO approved. Senso ingests the actual document and answers with citations, the gate is handed those rules, and the screen names the source it is enforcing (you can see "Acme Corp Corporate Air Travel Policy ACME-TRV-001 v1.4, verified" in our screenshots).

Two properties make it safe to put retrieval in front of money:

- **It can only tighten.** A retrieved policy that raises the cap, adds a cabin class, adds an airline or shortens the booking window is rejected, not applied. Nothing arriving over the network can widen spending authority. The worst case of a bad retrieval or a poisoned knowledge base is that the committed baseline is used; the second worst is that the agent is stricter than intended.
- **It cannot fail the booking.** Missing key, timeout, non-2xx, unparseable answer, schema violation and guard violation all fall back to the committed policy and record why. Resolution happens once at startup, so a booking never waits on retrieval.

Both are covered by automated tests rather than asserted.

One note for the Senso team: the ingest endpoint I needed, `POST /org/kb/raw`, is not in the public API reference. I found it in your published CLI bundle.

**Best Agentic User Experience**

The best decision was removing an interface. The first version had a text box and a Send button, and it made a compliance tool look like a flight search site. So the input became an inbound iMessage and the laptop screen became a console showing the policy, the decision and the audit log side by side. That leaves exactly one human action in the entire flow: a Face ID tap.

Four smaller choices:

- **The blocked screen is styled as a decision, not an error.** No red failure banner. It names each rule with its real numbers and the gap — "cabin class: business, policy allows economy only", "7,915.37 AUD, over by 6,615.37" — and states plainly that no payment session was created. It reads "the agent did not fail to pay, it declined to."
- **The search shows a live funnel**, 335 to 303 to 4, so you can see which rule cost you the flight instead of just a verdict.
- **No time estimate during the search.** A live search came back in 3.3s against the 8s I had assumed. An elapsed counter is honest at any speed; a written estimate is wrong at some of them.
- **The guardrail demo has a visible, labelled control**, because a rejection with no visible cause proves nothing.

Honesty is part of the interface too. The traveller's phone number is masked before it leaves the server, so it cannot reach a screenshot. And the screen states there is no override path in v1 rather than letting you discover it.

Harshad Karekar

### Parchi
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/sahayak-60e1) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/sreenathmmenon/parchi) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://app-production-8ee9.up.railway.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/yiyywJHtZEQ) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Be at the counter, wherever you are.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

WhatsApp turned out to be a dead end and we had to move channels mid-build.
Twilio's trial tier rejects free-form outbound with 422 and error 572002. The
console appeared to work, which cost us an hour, until we noticed the console
was sending a pre-approved template. Our approval message carries a photo, an
amount, a market comparison and a running total, so it can never be a
template. We moved to Telegram, which took five minutes, and kept the WhatsApp
adapter behind the same interface so it works the day the account is upgraded.

Visa rejected our payments and the error did not say why in plain terms. We
were generating payer email addresses ending in .local for internal use, and
Visa returned VIC_TRANSACTION_ERROR: Invalid Consumer Identity. Same class of
bug an hour later, where our local billing URL was being passed as merchant of
record. We split the internal API address from the public merchant identity,
which is what the network actually wants, and both went away.

We spent an evening on "billing merchant is unavailable" that was not an
outage at all. Our service key and the merchant service key had drifted apart,
so a 401 was surfacing as unavailability. We fixed the misleading error first,
gave authentication, missing invoice, amount mismatch and network failure
separate typed errors, and then the real cause was obvious in one line. We
also added a boot-time check so the two keys can never silently disagree
again.

Merchant onboarding was the design problem, not a bug. No Indian auto parts
retailer accepts a card credential submitted server to server. Shopify closed
its checkout APIs in April 2025 and Razorpay collects payment on the client.
Rather than fake a checkout, we changed who gets paid: the garage is the
merchant and settles an invoice, and the parts retailer's live catalogue is
used as the market reference price shown beside the bill. That turned a
blocker into the feature people react to, because you now see the markup at
the moment you are asked to approve it.

Our own bot rejected us. A first message from an unknown person was falling
past the entry checks into a rejection written for a different path, so a real
new user hit a wall. We fixed the cause rather than the message: first contact
is now the onboarding, and a payer's job page mints a connect code that binds
the requester's chat through the product's own link, with no manual database
edits.

The model was confidently wrong once and we caught it in evaluation. A brake
pad photo came back as a brake disc and matched to a Mercedes part. We fixed
the prompt and the matcher, and we deliberately did not lower the weak-match
threshold to make the number look better. Where nothing matches, the approval
says there is no reference price rather than inventing a comparison.

**The problem it solves**

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/83eea038367744b69205e3c1d67ed3af/599940c5-31c2-4370-9a23-e3adf01845a6.png)

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/83eea038367744b69205e3c1d67ed3af/4c5a8cf0-517b-401a-8ffd-9e40ad35374c.png)

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/83eea038367744b69205e3c1d67ed3af/41bc6b6d-d356-4c4e-b6a8-03a0a57a0d81.png)

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/83eea038367744b69205e3c1d67ed3af/0e62dfcd-1a74-43d4-86ff-305416301385.png)A lot of money in India is spent by one person and paid for by another. The
maid who is sent out for vegetables and comes back with a bill nobody can
check. The service advisor at the garage who calls you at work about a part
you cannot see. An old man in Kerala whose son sends money from Dubai every
week for medicines and groceries. A helper at a shop sent to buy stock. A
child sent to the corner store. All of it runs on phone calls, cash kept in a
drawer, and handing your card to somebody and hoping. The person paying feels
uneasy and says yes anyway. The person buying feels watched and gets blamed
when the amount looks wrong. Nobody has anything to point at afterwards.

Parchi puts a limit and a piece of evidence between them. The person paying
decides once, in advance, how much can be spent, on what, and for how long.
The person buying sends a photo or just speaks into their phone in their own
language, and never types a price. What reaches the payer is the photo, the
amount being charged, and what the same thing costs elsewhere on a live shop
catalogue. You can say yes in four seconds, or say no and the reason goes back
without your limits being revealed.

It matters now because agents can already buy things, but almost nobody buys
alone. The person paying stays in control without having to be present, and
the shop knows the money is confirmed and locked to them before they hand
anything over. Prava is what makes that true instead of a promise in our code.
An approval mints a one-time card locked to that shop for that exact amount,
and a request over the limit creates nothing at all.

Next: more shop categories, approvals that a family can see together instead
of one person, and the signed record becoming something a customer can carry
back to a shop when a bill is disputed.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

![Uploading image...]()The whole product is about permissions and controls on a card. The person paying sets a per-item limit, a total limit, who may ask, and for how long.

The credential that results is network-locked to one merchant and one amount.

The screen we are most proud of is the refusal, which shows the two numbers side by side and states plainly that no payment was created.

**OpenAI**

Used through the API for three things: identifying what is in a photo, transcribing voice notes including Hindi and mixed Hindi-English, and turning both into a plain sentence the person paying can read in four seconds. 

The model never produces a price. Prices come from live merchant catalogues, and where nothing matches well the approval says so instead of guessing.
We measure identification accuracy and over-limit detection against a keyword baseline rather than asserting it.

**iMessage Agent**

![Uploading image...]()iMessage is the payer's channel: the approval arrives from Parchi with a name and a picture rather than an unknown number, one message carries the whole lifecycle by editing in place, and a tapback registers the decision.

Built
against the Linq API and tested, pending our sandbox credentials.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/83eea038367744b69205e3c1d67ed3af/347413b3-4ceb-4709-8874-a7ad80383fa7.png)

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/83eea038367744b69205e3c1d67ed3af/fa6282ee-f4e5-4ce1-a98d-f74dccefd999.png)

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

Prava is the boundary this product is built on, not a checkout step at the
end. The policy gate runs before a session is ever created, so a refused
request produces no session and no credential anywhere. When a request is
permitted, the one-time credential is locked to a single merchant for a single
amount and expires in minutes, which is what makes it safe to let someone else
raise a spend at all. Take Prava out and the product does not degrade, it
stops existing. Live in sandbox on the deployed instance, ending in
report-status returning visa_confirmation Success.

### ReverseCart
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/reversecart-612e) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Priyammm05/reverseCart) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://reverse-cart.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/So1dLYsk0Tc) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Name your stay. Set your limit. Let hotels compete

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenAi](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenAi-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Finding a hotel usually means opening several websites, comparing inconsistent prices, checking distances, reading cancellation terms, and repeating the same search.

**ReverseCart reverses this process**. The buyer describes the stay once—location, dates, rooms, budget and preferences—and hotels compete with offers.

People can use it to:

- Find hotels near airports, offices, venues or landmarks.
- Compare price, distance, breakfast and cancellation terms together.
- Plan multi-city trips with one combined budget.
- Turn natural-language requests into structured booking requirements.
- Keep requests, offers, payments and confirmations in private history.
- Approve one exact purchase through Prava, with a fixed spending limit and no recurring charge.

This makes hotel discovery faster and purchasing safer because the buyer remains in control of the maximum amount, selected hotel and final payment approval.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest challenge was connecting multiple live systems into one reliable flow.

Hotel providers sometimes returned missing photos, unavailable rates or inconsistent location data. I handled this by separating verified hotel identity, live rate availability and fallback data, while clearly labelling simulated information.

Another challenge was preserving auctions and payments across refreshes. Initially, timers restarted and old payment sessions could be attached to another request. I fixed this by persisting auction deadlines, creating dedicated routes for saved markets, and binding every payment session to its request and reservation.

The Prava integration introduced an unusual status transition: credentials were reported as credentials_generated while the overall payment was awaiting_result. ReverseCart now recognizes credential readiness, performs the merchant checkout, reports the result back to Prava and updates the user’s private booking history.

I validated the complete journey with Playwright across desktop and mobile—from creating a request to receiving a confirmed sandbox booking.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

ReverseCart demonstrates the Visa Intelligent Commerce vision by enabling an AI-assisted hotel journey that continues from discovery to secure payment. After comparing hotel offers, the buyer approves one exact purchase through Prava’s Visa-powered payment flow. The generated credential is restricted by merchant, amount and time, while recurring payments are blocked. ReverseCart then executes the sandbox merchant checkout and reports the transaction outcome, preserving user control throughout the agent-initiated purchase.

**OpenAI**

ReverseCart uses OpenAI to convert an unstructured hotel request into a structured purchase mandate. The model extracts destinations, dates, number of rooms, guests, maximum budget, required conditions and optional preferences. This allows users to begin with one natural-language instruction instead of navigating multiple filters. If the OpenAI API is unavailable or reaches its usage limit, ReverseCart falls back to local parsing so the core workflow remains usable.

**Best Agentic User Experience**

ReverseCart replaces filters, comparison tabs and repetitive searches with one conversational request. It clearly shows what the agent understood, which hotels are competing, why an offer was recommended, its distance from the requested landmark and the final payment constraints. Users retain control through editable requirements, transparent comparisons, explicit approval and private booking history.

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

ReverseCart turns hotel booking into an agent-led purchasing workflow. A buyer describes their requirements in natural language, the system structures the request, discovers suitable hotels, compares competing offers and recommends the strongest trade-off. The selected purchase is then authorized through Prava using a scoped, one-time payment flow with a fixed spending limit and no recurring charges.

### Closet-Before-Cart (CBC)
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/closetbeforecart-cbc-6163) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/ajanaku1/closet-before-cart) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://closet-before-cart.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Prove the gap before buying

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenAi](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenAi-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest bug was the Prava handoff. iMessage previews could consume a one-time checkout link before the user opened it, which caused a "session already used" error. I fixed this with a CBC launch page that never opens checkout automatically, fresh quote IDs for retries, and idempotent payment callbacks. 

Merchant testing was also inconsistent, so CBC now fails safely when no exact size, colour, and budget match exists, and clearly labels the pinned sandbox item used in the demo.

**The problem it solves**

Getting dressed for an event often turns into buying something new, even when most of the outfit is already in your wardrobe. I built ClosetBeforeCart to help prevent unnecessary or impulsive spending. 

CBC checks a reference look against photos of your clothes in iMessage, tells you whether the outfit is complete, and identifies the one missing item if it is not. It only starts checkout for that proven gap, within the size and budget you approved.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

CBC uses Prava for its Visa Intelligent Commerce payment step. A signed Style Proof binds the missing item, and the exact $29 limit can be reached before checkout. The recorded sandbox transaction completed successfully and returned an approved result to CBC.

**Most Startup-Ready Product**

CBC is a live product with a clear path beyond the hackathon. It has working iMessage intake, a public Style Proof page, a tested payment flow, failure recovery, and 142 passing tests. The next step is to connect more live merchants and test it with real wardrobes.

**OpenAI**

CBC uses the OpenAI Responses API to understand one reference photo and six wardrobe photos. It turns them into structured garment evidence and generates an outfit preview. The model interprets the clothes, while tested rules decide whether the wardrobe is complete or one item is missing.

**iMessage Agent**

CBC runs inside iMessage through Linq. Users send their outfit and wardrobe photos, answer follow-up questions, and receive the payment link in the same conversation. The integration includes signed webhooks, replay protection, safe duplicate handling, and typing indicators.

**Best Agentic User Experience**

CBC works through iMessage, so users do not need another app or account. It shows typing while processing, asks only for missing details, and presents a visual Style Proof before checkout. Spending is limited to one proven wardrobe gap, with clear payment and recovery messages.

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

CBC completes a full agentic commerce flow. It reads wardrobe photos, decides whether anything is missing, collects the user’s size and budget, creates a proof-bound quote, and starts a Prava payment only after approval. The recorded sandbox transaction completed successfully.

### modular
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/modular-a199) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/mohammedsaadabdalla-svg/prava-modular-wallet) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> modular products

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Everything that slowed this project down, in one place — grouped by category and
ordered by how much it cost us. Where something still bites, the mitigation is noted.

---

## 1. Payment infrastructure (Prava sandbox) — highest friction

- **Visa network tokenization failures.** Hosted `vic/transact` returned
  `TOKEN_RESOLVE_ERROR: Could not resolve vProvisionedTokenId`; mandate charges came back
  Visa `DECLINED: expired authorization`. Network-level and outside app code — a healthy
  app still fails here.
- **Hardcoded 30s API timeout.** `prava-api.js` capped every request at 30s. A slow sandbox
  response flipped the state machine into `payment_session_unknown` (a deliberate no-retry
  state) even when the session had actually been created server-side.
- **API contract friction.** Guessed `POST /v1/checkout/sessions` → 404. Sent `totalAmount`
  → sandbox demanded `total_amount` + `purchase_context` (`VAL_2001`). The real contract
  lives in the SDK, not the docs.
- **Missing request signature.** A raw call to `/v1/wallet/shop/checkout` returns
  `AUTH_INVALID_SIGNATURE`; every wallet request must be Ed25519-signed with the agent key.
  The signing happens inside `wallet.js`, invisible to anyone calling the HTTP layer directly.
- **Session ownership scoping.** Passing `shopCheckout` a session minted under a different
  customer/agent returns `SHOP_SESSION_NOT_FOUND` — 404 on a valid id.

## 2. Agent identity

- **`AGENT_NOT_LINKED`.** No agent key (`~/.prava/agent.json`) or an unapproved link stops
  checkout before anything else — every wallet call signs with that key. This is exactly what
  broke the PR author's environment (missing `@prava-sdk/cli` / no agent key); the code was fine.
- **Delivery details gating.** A missing default address or contact phone blocks the quote
  entirely (`DELIVERY_DETAILS_REQUIRED`), so physical-goods checkout can't even begin.

## 3. LLM provider integration

- **Model access surprises.** The ChatGPT project key had no access to `gpt-4o` / `gpt-4o-mini`
  (`model_not_found`); only `gpt-5.6-sol` and `gpt-5.6-luna` were allowed.
- **`max_tokens` vs `max_completion_tokens`.** Newer models reject `max_tokens`
  (`unsupported_parameter`) and require `max_completion_tokens` instead.
- **Tools + reasoning conflict.** `gpt-5.6-sol` refuses function tools unless
  `reasoning_effort: 'none'` is set (or you move to `/v1/responses`).
- **Silent failures.** `callModel` had no HTTP status handling, so any API error came back as
  an empty assistant reply — this masked the model-access and token-param problems for a while.
  Now non-2xx responses emit an `agent.error` event instead.
- **Rate limiting.** The project is capped at 10k TPM. Each turn costs ~3900 input tokens
  (18-tool schema + history), so multi-turn checkout runs need ~1 request/minute spacing and
  hit `HTTP 429` mid-flow.
- **Model behavioural quirks.** `deepseek-v4-flash` would emit an empty `done` state with no
  tool calls; models would call `ask_user` and then not reliably continue after the answer.

## 4. Checkout state machine design

- **Human-in-the-loop is a hard rule.** The LLM can never authorize a payment — a passkey +
  UI confirm is required. The agent's job ends at `awaiting_approval`; anything claiming the
  model "approved" is by construction impossible.
- **Quote expiry.** Missing `expires_at` from a merchant → conservative 10-minute local expiry,
  so a quote can't silently become indefinitely payable.
- **Reusable, single-flight attempts.** `quoting → awaiting_confirmation →
  creating_payment_session → awaiting_approval → checkout_in_progress → paid`. A local state
  lock prevents a second payment session when the first request's network outcome is unknown.
- **Fresh-state resolution.** A variant missing from the product cache had to be re-fetched
  from Shopify and re-resolved rather than bouncing an error back to the model — the model
  otherwise just invents product/variant ids.

## 5. Interactive UI / AG-UI

- **Send-button bug.** The button's click handler passed the DOM event object into `send()`;
  fixed by checking `typeof overrideText === 'string'`.
- **`ask_user` wiring.** The form must surface as an `agent.interactive` event and the answers
  must come back as the next message; models don't reliably resume after it, so the prompt has
  to forbid guessing before the answer arrives.

## 6. Engineering & infrastructure

- **Port juggling.** Full-app on 3400, PR market agent on 3300, combined polished app on 3500.
  `market-page/server.js` must only bind when run directly (`process.argv[1]` guard), otherwise
  importing it as a module double-binds.
- **Process management.** Servers kept dying when the shell tool timed out; needed the
  `setsid nohup … & disown` pattern, and `pkill` races with restarts.
- **Headless environment.** No browser means the passkey/token flow can only be verified at the
  API level, never end-to-end visually.

## 7. Collaboration & Git

### PAR
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/par-2779) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/aayushdixit27/par-purchasing-agent) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://aayushdixit27.github.io/par-purchasing-agent/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/xzJFqBkfNE4) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Autonomous restocking that can say no.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

1. The sandbox went down mid-run and left our mandate paused. Every endpoint returned INTERNAL_ERROR. How you diagnosed it: a nonexistent mandate id also returned 500 instead of 404, which proved it was Prava and not our state. The damage: our pause had succeeded, the resume failed, and a paused mandate returns 409 on every charge, which looks identical to our own second beat firing when it should not. Fix: pause is now wrapped so its failure cannot end a run, and a run that cannot resume what it paused prints an ACTION NEEDED block naming the mandate.

2. One charge per weekly cycle, enforced inside Visa rather than in Prava. We requested max_charges: 10 and it was ignored. Visa returned Purchase already made in the current payment cycle. Our mandate's renewsAt was 9 August, a week past the deadline, so the live mint became unrepeatable and every rehearsal needed a fresh passkey ceremony inside a 900 second window. That is why the demo ships a seeded path and a recording.

3. A parser read a SKU as a price and nothing failed. An invoice was reworded to include the SKU, our regex skipped to the next number and landed on the identifier, and the transcript stated 8906087771593.00 per unit as fact. No exception, no empty result, no red test, in a build whose whole pitch is not stating unverified things as fact. Fix: anchored the capture past the identifier, then wrote a check asserting no SKU is ever printed as a price. It found all four instances in under a second and now runs on every preflight.

**The problem it solves**

Consider Maya. She's an owner and operator of a gym front desk in cafe, restocking at 11 p.m. from three supplier tabs and a paper par sheet. So, why has nobody automated this process before? It's not that the AI isn't smart enough. It's you would never give that AI your card.

So, the product is the permission slip, not the shopping one pass key, one rule twenty-four hundred a week, these suppliers, nothing more than ten percent above last paid.

What it then does that a price comparison cannot: chooses. Cheapest listing on screen loses, because the operator's own invoice says the "Pack Of 2" delivered one unit, so 269 each is really 538 each and the order moves to a different supplier.

Then the harder one: it refuses a purchase that cleared every rule, priced below what she last paid, because the invoice says a case is 12 and the listing says 24.

And the refusal sticks: the mandate is paused and the next charge comes back 409 MANDATE_NOT_ACTIVE from the network, so the block survives PAR being wrong or restarted.

If you remove verified context and the agent buys the most expensive option believing it is the cheapest, then buys a second thing every rule approved.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

PAR spends through Prava, which issues one-time merchant-scoped credentials on Visa rails. We ran the full lifecycle against the sandbox: created a mandate, approved it with a passkey, minted a credential, charged it and reported the result.

The part we care about is the refusal. When PAR finds a conflict it pauses the mandate, and the next charge on that supplier comes back 409 MANDATE_NOT_ACTIVE. So the block is enforced at the network, not in our software. If our code is wrong or restarted, the card is still off.

We also learned the limits are real rather than advisory. We asked for max_charges: 10 and Visa ignored it, returning "Purchase already made in the current payment cycle." The cap and the merchant lock are enforced inside the network, which is exactly why we put the rules that Visa cannot express into our own gate.

**Agent Commerce Discovery & Trust**

The operator's invoices, receipts and par sheet are ingested into Senso. PAR queries Senso before it is allowed to spend, and every decision carries the document it came from.

Senso does not just block bad purchases here, it picks the supplier. A face wash listed at INR 538 for a "Pack Of 2" looks like the cheapest option at 269 a unit. The operator's own invoice says she paid 538 and one bottle arrived. So it is 538 a unit, it drops from first to last, and the order moves to a different supplier. Remove Senso and there is no invoice to divide by, so the agent buys the most expensive option believing it is the cheapest.

It also catches the purchase no rule could catch. One order cleared every rule the operator wrote, and was priced below what she last paid, so no price rule could ever have stopped it. Senso returned the invoice saying a case is 12 units where the listing said 24, and PAR refused and cited the document.

One gap worth naming: context search returns the quote and the document identity but no document date. We supply the date at ingest and label it in our output as supplied by us, because provenance without a date cannot support "your invoice from June says otherwise."

### LaterCart
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/latercart-4c09) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Pranav-Bobde/latercart) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://latercart.vercel.app) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtube.com/shorts/tZrJN3lFzgs) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Reorders in iMessage, approved one at a time

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenAi](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenAi-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

1. **Sandbox vs production boundaries.** Prava’s CLI session command emits production links, so I split sandbox REST payments from signed wallet/UCP operations and added startup guards that reject production hosts or keys.

2. **Serverless native checkout.** I replaced the local CLI dependency with an Ed25519 signed-fetch client, then proved request parity against captured CLI fixtures—including inconsistent price units between search and variants.

3. **Durable schedules without duplicate payments.** Vercel Workflows sleeps until execution; every run wake-checks status, version, and occurrence. Payment steps have platform retries disabled, plus a DB lock and idempotency keys.

4. **Real iMessage delivery.** I captured a Linq webhook, verified its Standard Webhooks signature, added replay deduplication, typing indicators, tapbacks, and failure-safe replies.

5. **Unknowns and a sandbox rate limit.** The recorded app run reached approval, mandate creation, and credential mint before Prava returned HTTP 429. LaterCart did not blind-retry: it explained the cause, consequence, and next action in iMessage, recorded the state in the timeline, and asked for reconciliation only if the merchant outcome was genuinely unknown. The Prava team acknowledged the sandbox-side issue and explicitly approved this validated scope for the hackathon demo.

6. **Closing the Senso loop safely.** Checkout evidence is sanitized by a schema that forbids payment and user data, ingested until searchable, then retrieved during the next merchant preflight.

**The problem it solves**

Repeat purchases are fragmented across merchant-specific subscriptions: cadence options, controls, and terminology differ; changes live in separate settings pages; and payment authority is often standing rather than scoped to one order. LaterCart replaces that with fresh, user-approved scheduled purchases through one iMessage interface, flexible schedules, a live product and price check, and payment authority limited to the single approved purchase. Senso grounds recommendations and learns from sanitized checkout outcomes; the web timeline explains every step. Coffee is the first validated category, not the product boundary—next, I want to add more capability-verified UCP merchants.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

Prava is the payment spine: UCP product and quote verification, a scoped one-time sandbox mandate, hosted passkey approval, credential mint, native shop checkout, and explicit APPROVED or DECLINED reporting. LaterCart disables automatic checkout retries, uses payment locks, and rejects production hosts or keys. Separate sandbox smoke tests reached terminal merchant declines. The recorded app run reached approval and mint before Prava returned HTTP 429; LaterCart explained the cause, consequence, and next action without a blind retry. The Prava team acknowledged the sandbox-side issue and explicitly greenlit this validated scope for the hackathon demo. Additional merchants are enabled only after their required operations pass validation.

**OpenAI**

The OpenAI API, through AI SDK, performs two bounded jobs: converting natural-language messages into schema-validated reminder commands, and ranking only supplied UCP, Senso, and preference candidates with cited sources. It never decides price, payment, checkout, or retries; those remain deterministic code.

**iMessage Agent**

iMessage is LaterCart’s control plane: create and confirm reminders, pause, skip, resume or cancel, receive the Prava approval link, follow progress, retry safely, resolve unknown outcomes, and receive the final result. A real Linq webhook signature is verified, and typing indicators plus tapbacks were live-tested.

**Agent Commerce Discovery & Trust**

LaterCart uses Senso before commerce to retrieve grounded product and merchant context for cited recommendations, and after commerce to ingest sanitized MerchantExecutionEvidence. This closed loop is live-verified: checkout evidence reached searchable ready state and was retrieved by the next Stumptown preflight. Live price and stock are always refreshed from UCP.

**Best Agentic User Experience**

LaterCart turns complex states—scheduled, checking, approval needed, declined, rate-limited, or uncertain—into a calm iMessage plus a transparent signed timeline. Typing indicators show work in progress, tapbacks acknowledge commands, and every failure states the cause, consequence, and next action. Checkout is never silently retried, so the user stays in control.

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

LaterCart is an agentic commerce workflow from natural-language intent and durable scheduling to grounded product discovery, scoped user approval, native checkout, and truthful recovery. It connects Linq, OpenAI, Senso, UCP and Prava, Effect, PostgreSQL, and Vercel Workflows in one user-controlled purchase journey.

### Giftwrap
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/giftwrap-0d23) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Chokkam99/giftwrap) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://giftwrap-1jsc-rho.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> The agent picks the gift. The card caps the spend.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Playwright](https://img.shields.io/badge/Playwright-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Giving a real gift is awkward when you do not know someone's exact taste, size, or preferred store. A gift card is easier, but it locks them into one place.

GiftWrap lets a buyer set the person, budget, stores, and a note in plain language. They can pick an item themselves, or send the recipient a link to choose within that budget. The agent searches six real Shopify catalogs concurrently over UCP and returns one merged, budgeted shortlist instead of a pile of store tabs. Prava then mints a one-time card scoped to that single merchant and capped at the approved amount, the buyer approves it with a passkey, and a browser session completes the real checkout.

The safety boundary sits below the model. The budget and merchant limits are enforced in code before any payment client is touched, and again by the card itself at the network level. A scripted red-team run refuses an over-budget mint, a card replayed at the wrong merchant, and a checkout aimed at a real store instead of our dev store, each one before the relevant client is even loaded. The card credential lives in server-side state and never enters a prompt, a tool result, or a log.

The recipient link is deliberately thin: it carries the note, the budget and the catalog, never the buyer's conversation, and the recipient never gets tool access.

Next, we want to take the recipient handoff into more messaging channels and add more stores.

**Challenges we ran into**

Prava wiring that lied about being healthy. Our first integration looked fine but quietly fell back to fake data when a client signature did not match. We tore out the silent fallback: every degraded or stubbed call is now logged with its traceback, flagged in the tool result the model sees, and reported by /health, so "is this real?" is a question you can answer in one request. We also found Prava's revoke endpoint needs an explicit {} JSON body when the request carries a JSON content type.

Two Shopify checkout problems that looked like one. Shopify renders a hidden autofill_* decoy copy of every shipping address input, so our early automation typed into fields that silently discarded the text. Separately, Shopify gives each card input its own iframe with an identical generic name, so a normal selector lands in the wrong frame. We exclude the decoys by id prefix and route every card field to the frame that actually owns it. We rehearsed both an approved and a declined Bogus Gateway flow.

The catalog filter we should not have trusted. Shopify's UCP price filter is a soft relevance hint, not a constraint: a live query capped at Rs 3,000 came back with items at Rs 3,799, Rs 5,199 and Rs 7,999. If we had trusted it, the agent would have shown a buyer things it could not pay for. We now re-enforce the budget in our own code before anything reaches the model or the mint call. On one recipient-facing search that second filter dropped 10 of 13 results.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

Prava is the core trust layer. GiftWrap creates a one-time session for one merchant and one approved amount, sends the buyer through hosted passkey approval, then uses the returned payment credential only for that checkout.

The credential lives in server-side state and never enters a prompt, a tool result, or a log. The budget is enforced twice: once in our own code before minting, and again by the card itself at the network level, so a compromised or misbehaving agent still cannot authorize a charge above the approved amount.

**Most Startup-Ready Product**

This is aimed at a real, common moment: buying a thoughtful gift without guessing. The spending limit and merchant scope make an agent's purchase authority understandable, while the recipient-choice link solves the "I do not know what they want" problem.

The agent brain is provider-agnostic behind one environment variable, so the product is not tied to a single model vendor's pricing or availability.

**OpenAI**

OpenAI powers the live gift-planning and tool-use conversation. It turns buyer intent into UCP catalog searches, budgeted options, and the approval flow.

We verified a real OpenAI-backed chat flow end to end in the app: an opening request, a concurrent multi-store search returning twelve in-budget products from live catalogs, an approved product, a scoped mint attempt, and the recipient-choice path where the model reads a pick back to the buyer.

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

GiftWrap turns a natural-language gifting request into real catalog search, product choice, approval, and checkout. The agent can act, but its payment authority is physically limited by the card it receives.

### EatSmart
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/eatsmart-a585) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Autonomous Grocery & Meal Planning Agent

![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Mapping meal plans to real grocery products

Meal planning produces ingredients like "paneer" or "whole wheat flour," but grocery platforms list products with different brands, package sizes, and naming conventions. We had to normalize ingredient names and design a mapping layer so the agent could consistently find the correct products.

Price comparison across stores

Different grocery platforms often sell the same product in different quantities and at different prices. Instead of comparing products directly, we standardized units and evaluated cost-per-unit to recommend the most economical option while keeping the total order within the user's budget.

Orchestrating multiple agent tasks

The workflow consists of several dependent stages—meal planning, nutrition analysis, grocery extraction, price comparison, and cart creation. Ensuring each stage passed structured data to the next without breaking the pipeline required careful API design and validation.

Keeping the experience responsive

Since multiple AI and shopping operations can take time, we added a staged progress interface ("Planner → Nutrition → Shopping") so users can see exactly what the agent is doing instead of waiting on a blank loading screen.

**The problem it solves**

Planning healthy meals while staying within a budget is surprisingly time-consuming. People often have to:

Decide what to cook every day.
Calculate calories, protein, and nutrition manually.
Compare grocery prices across multiple stores.
Create shopping lists and purchase items separately.

This process becomes even harder for students, working professionals, fitness enthusiasts, and families trying to eat healthier without overspending.

What EatSmart does

EatSmart is an autonomous grocery planning agent that turns a simple goal into a complete shopping plan.

The user only provides:

Dietary preference (Vegetarian, Vegan, etc.)
Nutrition goal (High Protein, Weight Loss, Balanced Diet)
Budget
Duration
Location

The agent then automatically:

Generates a personalized multi-day meal plan.
Calculates daily nutrition (calories, protein, carbs, fats).
Builds the exact grocery list required.
Compares prices across supported grocery platforms.
Selects the most cost-effective combination.
Prepares a ready-to-checkout cart.

Instead of spending an hour planning meals and shopping, users receive an optimized plan in seconds.

### Enchanto-AI
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/enchantoai-9d8c) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/rajdeep13-coder/Enchanto) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/30K5I0a1P2E) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/jESNf6PwqDg?si=P5ADAAY7bWnOPH-X) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-HexaFalls%202-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hexafalls2.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Your Autonomous Wizard for Consumer Justice

![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![Google API](https://img.shields.io/badge/Google%20API-333333?style=flat-square) ![Neo4j](https://img.shields.io/badge/Neo4j-333333?style=flat-square) ![LangGraph](https://img.shields.io/badge/LangGraph-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. Agents contradicting each other**

Because Enchanto runs multiple specialized agents (research, evidence, strategy, drafting) instead of one big prompt, we initially hit a problem where the research agent would surface one regulation, but the drafting agent would cite it slightly wrong or draw a different conclusion from it — since each agent only sees a summary of the previous agent's output, not its full reasoning.

**2. Hallucinated citations before we added retrieval grounding**

Early on, when we prompted Gemini directly without a retrieval layer in front of it, it would confidently invent regulation numbers and case precedents that sounded completely plausible but didn't exist — the exact failure mode that got other "AI legal helper" tools in trouble.

**3. Gemini's function-calling schema didn't map cleanly onto our existing agent structure**

Since Enchanto's original pipeline was built around a different model's function-calling format, switching to Gemini meant our agent handoffs and tool schemas needed reworking — small differences in how Gemini expects structured output broke the pipeline in subtle ways at first.

**4. Making a multi-service architecture demo-reliable**

Our original setup relied on separate services for the vector store, knowledge graph, and cache — great for production, risky for a live hackathon demo on venue wifi where any one service failing kills the whole flow.


**5. Time pressure: choosing depth over breadth**

With 24 hours, we had to decide between making the pipeline work shallowly across every domain we listed (insurance, banking, telecom, airlines) or making one domain — health insurance — work really well end-to-end with real citations.

**The problem it solves**

Getting denied — a claim, a refund, a dispute — is easy. Fighting back is hard, and that difficulty is the whole business model for a lot of institutions.

Health insurers denied 19% of in-network claims in 2024 (~85 million rejections on ACA plans alone), yet fewer than 1% of people ever appeal.
When people do appeal, they win 70–80%+ of the time — the problem was never a weak case, it was never knowing where to start.
The same pattern repeats everywhere: banks reversing chargebacks only if you push, airlines stalling refund requests, telecoms burying cancellation fees in fine print. Companies aren't betting you're wrong — they're betting you'll give up.

Enchanto exists to remove that asymmetry. It gives an ordinary person the same research, evidence-gathering, and argument-building power that used to require a lawyer or hours of frustrated Googling — compressed into minutes.

.

**How It Makes This Easier and Safer**

*Easier:*
No legal knowledge required — you upload a rejection letter (even a photo of it), Enchanto figures out which regulations and precedents apply, not you.
Minutes, not hours — what normally means digging through policy PDFs and government sites happens automatically.
One tool, every domain — you don't need a different app for insurance vs. banking vs. airlines; the same pipeline adapts to each.

*Safer:*
Every claim is cited, not just plausible-sounding — so you (or a real lawyer, if it escalates that far) can verify each argument before it's sent, instead of trusting a black box.
Grounded in retrieved regulations and precedent, not guessed from a language model's memory — reducing the hallucinated-citation risk that's sunk other "AI legal helper" tools.
You stay in control — Enchanto drafts, you review and send. It's an advocate that arms you, not an autopilot that acts without your sign-off.

**Accio Relevance - Build with Actian VectorAI Database**

**How Enchanto Used Actian (VectorAI Database)**
What it powers: the research agent's retrieval layer

Enchanto's research agent needs to find the exact regulation, policy clause, or precedent relevant to a user's specific denial — not just generically related documents. We used Actian's VectorAI Database to store embeddings of regulatory text, policy language, and prior appeal outcomes, and query it for semantically relevant matches against the extracted denial reason.

Ingestion: We embedded a corpus of insurance regulations, consumer protection statutes, and appeal precedents into Actian VectorAI
Query time: the denial reason + policy details are embedded and matched against this store to retrieve the top-k most relevant sources
Grounding: only retrieved, verifiable text is passed to the drafting agent — this is what prevents hallucinated citations


**Why This Is the Best Use Case for Actian**

1. Relevance search is the actual bottleneck we needed to solve.
The hardest part of building a trustworthy appeal isn't writing persuasive text — it's finding the right regulation out of thousands. That's precisely the "Accio Relevance" problem Actian's track is built around, not a bolted-on integration to chase a prize.

2. Retrieval quality directly determines whether the product is safe to use.
A weak vector match means a wrong citation means a user submits an appeal citing a regulation that doesn't apply to their case. Actian isn't a nice-to-have here — it's the component standing between "helpful tool" and "confidently wrong tool."

3. It's the backbone of a multi-domain product, not a single lookup table.
As Enchanto expands beyond health insurance into banking, telecom, and airlines, Actian VectorAI is what lets the same research agent scale across domains — swap the embedded corpus, not the architecture.

**Best Use of ElevenLabs**

**How Enchanto Used ElevenLabs**
What it powers: accessible, human explanations of dense legal language

Insurance and legal denials are written in language most people find intimidating or hard to parse — especially elderly users or anyone with visual impairments. We used ElevenLabs' text-to-speech to let users hear a plain-language explanation of their denial and their draft appeal read back to them, instead of only reading dense text on screen.



**Why This Is the Best Use Case for ElevenLabs**

1. It directly serves the users who need it most.
The people most likely to give up on a denial without appealing are often the least equipped to parse legal text — elderly patients, non-native speakers, people with visual impairments. Voice isn't a gimmick here; it's an accessibility feature aimed squarely at the population this product exists for.

2. It builds trust before a high-stakes action.
Sending an appeal is a one-shot, consequential action. Hearing it read aloud — in a natural, human voice rather than a robotic TTS — gives users a final, comfortable check before they submit something with real consequences.

3. It fits the product's actual values.
Enchanto's whole pitch is "an advocate, not a black box." A calm, human voice walking someone through their situation reinforces that positioning far better than another wall of text would.

**Best Use of MongoDB Atlas**

**How Enchanto Used MongoDB Atlas**
What it powers: case history, user state, and escalation tracking

Enchanto isn't a single-shot letter generator — a real dispute often involves multiple rounds (initial appeal → rejection → escalation → ombudsman). We used MongoDB Atlas as the persistence layer to store:

Case documents: the original denial, extracted details, retrieved evidence, and generated drafts per user
Escalation timelines: deadlines and next steps per case (e.g., statutory response windows)
Conversation/session state: so the agent pipeline has memory of what's already been argued if a case needs a second round



**Why This Is the Best Use Case for MongoDB Atlas**

1. Real disputes aren't single-turn — persistence is core to the product, not an add-on.
A tool that forgets everything after one letter isn't actually an advocate. MongoDB Atlas is what lets Enchanto track a case across weeks of back-and-forth, which is the difference between a demo trick and a usable product.

2. Flexible schema matches genuinely varied data.
A health insurance case, a bank dispute, and an airline refund claim all have wildly different fields and evidence types. MongoDB's document model lets us store all of them without forcing an artificial one-size-fits-all schema.

3. It's the operational backbone that makes the multi-agent pipeline stateful.
Vector retrieval (Actian) finds the right sources; MongoDB Atlas remembers what happened and what's next. Both are necessary — one without the other leaves either a stateless smart search engine or a database with no intelligence behind it.

**Best Use of Gemini API**

**How Enchanto Used the Gemini API**
1. Multimodal input — reading the actual denial letter
Instead of asking users to retype their rejection letter, Enchanto lets them upload a photo or scan of it directly. Gemini's native multimodal understanding reads the image and extracts the denial reason, policy number, and relevant clauses — no separate OCR step needed.

2. The reasoning core of each agent
Each stage of the pipeline — research, evidence-gathering, strategy, drafting — is a separate Gemini call with a narrow, specific prompt and its own context, rather than one giant prompt trying to do everything:

Research agent: takes the extracted denial reason and retrieves/reasons over relevant regulations and precedent
Evidence agent: cross-references the user's policy details against what was retrieved
Strategy agent: decides the strongest angle of argument given the evidence
Drafting agent: writes the final appeal in a persuasive, professional register, inserting citations inline

3. Function calling for structured, verifiable output
Rather than letting Gemini free-write a letter, we used function calling / structured output so the model returns a structured object — {claim, citation, source_confidence} — for every argument it makes. That structure is what lets the UI show a citation confidence badge next to each claim, instead of just a wall of prose the user has to blindly trust.

4. Long context for grounding
Gemini's large context window let us feed retrieved regulation text and prior case excerpts directly into the prompt for the research and drafting steps, rather than relying on the model's memorized (and hallucination-prone) knowledge of insurance law.


**Why This Is a Strong Use Case for the Gemini API**

1. It uses Gemini for what it's actually good at, not just "because it's an LLM."
A lot of hackathon Gemini integrations are a single chat wrapper. Enchanto uses Gemini across four distinct reasoning roles in one pipeline, each with a different job — that's a genuine showcase of orchestrating the model as a reasoning engine, not just a chatbot backend.

2. Multimodal input isn't decorative — it's the entry point of the whole product.
The user's very first interaction (uploading a photo of a denial letter) depends on Gemini's vision capability. Remove it, and the product doesn't work at all — that's a much stronger "use case" story than a feature bolted on afterward.

3. Structured output is what makes the output trustworthy.
Function calling turns Gemini from "writes a nice-sounding letter" into "produces a citation-checkable legal document" — which is the entire differentiator of the product versus a plain chatbot. Judges evaluating "best use of Gemini API" are usually looking for exactly this: does the API capability unlock the product idea, or is it interchangeable with any other model?

4. Real-world stakes make reliability the point, not a footnote.
This isn't a toy app — a hallucinated citation in a real appeal letter has real consequences for a user. Grounding Gemini's output with retrieval and forcing structured, sourced responses is a genuine demonstration of building responsibly on top of the API, not just impressively.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![SolanaSDK](https://img.shields.io/badge/SolanaSDK-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

While modern AI agents can automate complex workflows and manage multi-system operations, none can safely execute real-world financial transactions. Today, users increasingly rely on LLMs to discover and compare products instead of manually browsing e-commerce sites, but a major gap remains: agents cannot complete the purchase. JarvisPayz bridges this gap by enabling AI agents to not only search and recommend products across user-authorized stores, but also directly execute purchases on their behalf. Built on the Solana blockchain, every transaction is fully transparent and traceable on-chain, while smart contracts strictly enforce user-defined budget caps to prevent unauthorized spending or agent overreach.

**Challenges we ran into**

Fine-Tuning & Orchestrating the Multi-Agent System: Designing a multi-agent workflow where specialized agents handle distinct tasks such as store discovery, catalog querying, basket management, and transaction policy verification - proved extremely challenging. Ensuring smooth context sharing and deterministic agent execution without hallucinations or lost state required extensive prompt engineering and state machine tuning.

Building Truly Personalized User Agents: Personalizing the agent to understand individual user preferences, connected stores, and spend limits while strictly adhering to OAuth boundaries was tough. We had to ensure the agent only queries stores the user explicitly authorized, maintains long-term user context securely, and never triggers an unapproved payment flow.

**Best Use of Gemini API**

1. Autonomous Agent On-Chain Payment Execution (Top Feature)
While traditional AI integrations stop at text generation or simple recommendations, JarvisPayz uses the Gemini API to autonomously construct, verify, and execute real-world on-chain payments. Gemini acts as the financial agent—translating natural language requests into precise, machine-executable checkout intents, validating cart totals against merchant invoices, and triggering automated payments on the Stellar blockchain.

2. Multi-Agent Orchestration & Deterministic Intent Parsing
Executing financial payments on-chain leaves zero room for AI hallucination. We rely on Gemini to power a multi-agent workflow that parses complex user queries into structured search parameters, multi-query catalog retrieval, cart updates, and execution payloads with strict JSON schema compliance.

3. AI-Driven Personalization & Behavioral Memory
Gemini continuously processes past user interactions and purchase history to build structured, long-term shopping profiles. It evaluates product candidates against the user's specific brand affinities, past buying habits, and budget preferences to deliver highly customized recommendation explanations.

4. Safe AI Reasoning Guardrailed by Smart Contracts
JarvisPayz showcases a benchmark pattern for agentic AI: combining Gemini’s autonomous decision-making with smart-contract enforcement. Gemini autonomously manages product selection and basket compilation, while on-chain smart contracts act as a deterministic firewall enforcing strict daily budget caps and transaction verification before funds can move.

**Best Use of Solana**

Why JarvisPayz is the Best Use of Solana

1. Sub-Second Finality and Micro-Fees for E-Commerce
E-commerce checkouts demand instant gratification and friction-free payment confirmation. Traditional block times or high gas fees make real-time AI shopping checkouts impractical. Solana's sub-second finality and sub-penny transaction costs make immediate, automated checkouts computationally and economically viable for conversational AI flows.

2. On-Chain Spend Policy Enforced via Rust Smart Contracts
To solve the critical trust issue of AI agents spending funds, we built on-chain policy guardrails using Rust smart contracts deployed on Solana (TrustList and PDA wallet). Instead of relying on vulnerable off-chain database limits, parameters like daily spend limits, maximum per-transaction caps, merchant allowlists, and unique purchase intent verifications are cryptographically enforced on-chain before any transfer can execute.

3. Dedicated Per-User Smart Accounts
Each shopper receives their own dedicated, secure Agent Smart Wallet instance on Solana. This removes the need for centralized escrows or pooled wallets, ensuring direct wallet-to-merchant peer-to-peer payments and keeping user funds isolated and secure.

4. Impeccable Cryptographic Receipts and Reconciliation
By settling checkouts on Solana, every purchase produces an immutable cryptographic receipt. This provides both the merchant and the consumer with instantly verifiable proofs of payment (via Solana Explorer transaction hashes) linked to automated, double-spend-protected merchant reconciliation pipelines.
