### Pavlos
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/pavlos-cc7f) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-HyperFusion-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hyperfusion.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Guardrails for AI agents that touch money.

![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![SQLAlchemy](https://img.shields.io/badge/SQLAlchemy-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Building Pavlos required moving beyond standard LLM testing to construct a mathematically rigorous, multi-sector financial stress laboratory:

Challenge 1: Paired Monte Carlo Simulation with Common Random Numbers (CRN)
Problem: Comparing an unguarded agent against a guarded control in separate stochastic runs introduces high variance (noise from random timing, different prompt outcomes, or network drops), making it hard to prove whether a safety policy actually prevented a failure.
Solution: We engineered a Paired Monte Carlo engine (sector_simulation.py) using Common Random Numbers (CRN). By seeding a single stress vector and replaying it twice—once inside an unguarded counterfactual and once with the deterministic Money-Movement Guard—both runs experience identical faults, network timeouts, stale state, and beneficiary identity drift. This isolates true causal impact and allows computing Wilson 95% Score Confidence Intervals for failure rates, residual ambiguity, and false holds.
Challenge 2: Decoupling MiroFish World Graphs from Financial Accounting
Problem: Agent interactions require realistic world modeling (actor memories, partial information, relationship graphs, temporal pressure), but relying on a graph or LLM memory as a ledger leads to severe balance drift.
Solution: We established a strict architectural boundary: The graph is never a ledger. We used a MiroFish-inspired world graph for actor visibility and scenario generation (worldgen.py), while keeping 100% of financial state, double-entry balance rules (Debits = Credits), and idempotency reservations inside deterministic Python code (ledger.py & guard.py).
Challenge 3: Expanding Across 5 Distinct Financial Sectors
Problem: Financial consequences differ radically across domains—a refund is compensatable/reversible, whereas an outbound treasury wire or paper stock order is irreversible.
Solution: We built 5 domain-specific World Packs (agent_catalog.py) with specialized state machines, authority envelopes, and harm oracles:
Payments: Refund & Reconciliation (Stripe, Adyen targets)
Lending: Hardship Servicing & Repayment Schedules (LoanPro, Mambu, Plaid)
Corporate Treasury: Beneficiary-Bound Outbound Wires (Modern Treasury)
Insurance: Claims Payout Execution (Guidewire ClaimCenter)
Investing: Paper Portfolio Rebalancing (Alpaca Paper, DriveWealth)
Challenge 4: Zero-Dependency Architecture & Local Security Isolation
Problem: Financial stress labs require absolute isolation so that simulation code can never accidentally hit live production bank/PSP APIs or leak API credentials.
Solution: We built Pavlos using 100% pure Python standard library with zero external pip dependencies. The system runs paper-only sandboxes, refuses live account modes, binds strictly to local loopback (127.0.0.1), and keeps LLM keys strictly in memory during optional Azure OpenAI world compilation.

**The problem it solves**

As AI agents transition from sending emails to managing real-world financial operations—initiating payments, issuing refunds, adjusting account ledgers, waiving fees, or approving credit—they enter a domain where errors have direct economic identity and catastrophic financial risk.

Generic LLM tracing tools (like Langfuse or Phoenix) log prompts and tool calls, but fail to secure or explain financial actions:

Language is Not Authorization: Standard agents allow LLM text outputs to directly call money-moving APIs. A malicious prompt injection (e.g., the Grok–Bankrbot incident), quoted text, or compromised dashboard (e.g., AIXBT) can trick a model into transferring real money or tokens.
"Success" is Not Binary: In finance, an API timeout doesn't mean a payment failed. Retrying an ambiguous request can double-debit an account or double-refund a customer. Traditional tools collapse complex financial lifecycles into simple SUCCESS / FAILED flags, ignoring provider acknowledgments, settlement cutoffs, and reconciliation suspense.
Correct Math vs. Wrong Economics: A double-entry ledger can balance perfectly while paying the wrong beneficiary, using the wrong currency exponent, or violating customer mandates (e.g., the Citi–Revlon $894M wire error).
No Safe Environment for Failure Testing: Engineering teams cannot safely test how an agent handles edge cases (like rate limits, gas spikes, duplicate webhooks, or stale fraud lists) directly against live financial APIs without risking real money loss.

**The problem it solves**

Micro-enterprises and freelancers face massive administrative fragmentation. Tracking real-time, multi-state Indian tax rules (split CGST, SGST, and IGST) usually require complex software, while verifying legal contracts and managing daily execution flows introduce high data-leakage risks and expensive subscription overhead.

This suite solves these issues by bringing localized, privacy-first automation onto client-side hardware:
* **Bypasses expensive cloud processing:** Runs LLMs (Gemini 1.5 Flash) directly in browser memory via user-supplied API tokens to eliminate server costs. 
* **Eliminates calculation errors:** Prevents manual tax split calculation mistakes through a smart, granular GST invoicing dashboard.
* **Ensures absolute data privacy:** Financial logs and sensitive client documents stay 100% on the user's local machine.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/caa605ebd8d842919d83cebeb88d93ac/40cbd5b0-2385-451c-b327-fe248b20b18f.png)

**Challenges we ran into**

* **State Tax Split Edge Cases:** Implementing compliant dynamic calculations for cross-border transactions (IGST) versus localized split parameters (CGST + SGST) required strict mathematical rounding validation to accurately match Indian financial standards.

* **Zero-Cloud LLM Client Security:** Forcing Gemini 1.5 Flash to pull keys securely from localized browser storage without relying on heavy backend infrastructure required implementing explicit, sandboxed asynchronous client-side context safety boundaries.

### StartStep
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/startstep-24d7) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1-EtITnZp0VYIy_IJbxjrtTPVTse3s5ER/view?usp=sharing) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtube.com/shorts/cXKLZN_JH6s) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Dora%20Hack%202.0-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://dora-hack.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Tiny steps. Real starts. Big change. StartStep

![Kotlin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kotlin-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Building StartStep involved several non-trivial challenges:

Latency: Voice conversations feel awkward if responses take too long. We optimized prompts and networking to achieve near real-time interactions.
Prompt reliability: LLMs naturally produce helpful but sometimes overly ambitious advice. We had to iteratively refine prompts to force ultra-small first actions.
Speech recognition edge cases: Handling partial transcripts, silence timeouts, microphone permissions, and noisy environments required significant testing.
Audio synchronization: Coordinating Lottie mascot states with streaming TTS playback and waveform visualization was surprisingly complex.
Emotional tone: Productivity apps often become accidentally judgmental. We repeatedly tested wording to ensure every message remained supportive and non-shaming.
Background notifications: Triggering helpful reminders only when a user truly disengaged from an active task required careful lifecycle management.

**The problem it solves**

StartStep was inspired by a very common ADHD experience: knowing exactly what needs to be done, yet feeling physically unable to begin. Traditional productivity apps assume that motivation appears first and action follows. For many ADHD users, the opposite is true—action must become tiny enough that the brain stops treating it as a threat.

We wanted to build a tool that felt less like a task manager and more like a compassionate friend sitting beside you saying, “Let’s just do the first 15 seconds together.” The goal was not maximizing output; it was reducing shame, lowering activation energy, and helping users experience the momentum of starting.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges We Ran Into

During the development of CareBridge AI, we faced several challenges, especially while turning our initial idea into a working application. One major challenge was integrating the frontend with Supabase and moving from demo/local storage data to a proper database with authentication, privacy controls, and secure data access. We also had to learn and work with new AI development tools such as Lovable, Claude, and Google AI Studio, while understanding how different tools could work together. Another hurdle was building a continuous decision loop where the system could observe new information, reassess its previous decisions, and adapt its actions as conditions changed. We addressed this by structuring the system around continuous observation, reasoning, risk assessment, capital allocation, execution, outcome monitoring, and adaptation.

We also had to ensure that decisions remained within explicit capital and risk limits, rather than allowing the AI to act solely on predicted returns.

**The problem it solves**

Our project addresses the security risks introduced by autonomous AI agents performing financial transactions, where traditional authentication verifies an agent’s identity and permissions but may not determine whether its actual action matches the authorized role, financial policies, and intended objective. We propose an **AI-powered, intent-aware security layer** that verifies the agent’s identity and authority, decodes and interprets the proposed transaction, evaluates it against predefined financial policies, simulates its potential state changes, and analyzes whether the transaction is consistent with the intended action. The core innovation is moving beyond simply asking **“Is this agent authorized?”** to asking **“Is this authorized agent performing the correct action for the intended purpose?”**, providing an additional layer of protection against unintended, malicious, or policy-violating financial transactions.

**The problem it solves**

# What Problem This Project Solves

Most adaptive traffic signal control today runs on reinforcement learning (RL) 
policies trained to optimize traffic flow. These policies are fast and 
efficient for everyday traffic, but they're fundamentally reflexive — they 
react to patterns they've seen before, without actually understanding **what's 
happening** in a scene.

When something unusual occurs — an ambulance approaching, a pedestrian caught 
mid-crossing, an accident blocking a lane — a policy trained purely on 
historical traffic data has no way to reason about the situation or judge the 
right response. It just keeps optimizing for the metric it was trained on, 
which can make emergencies worse (for example, holding a green light for 
maximum throughput exactly when an ambulance needs the intersection cleared).

## How VLMLight Solves This

VLMLight combines two decision-making systems instead of relying on one:

- **A fast RL policy** handles routine traffic — everyday queuing, cycle 
  changes, normal flow — where speed and efficiency matter more than deep 
  reasoning.
- **A vision-language reasoning branch** takes over for safety-critical or 
  ambiguous scenes. It actually *looks* at the intersection through a 
  multi-view visual simulator (bird's-eye view plus four directional camera 
  feeds), uses a vision-language model to understand what's happening, and a 
  language model to reason step by step about the right signal response.
- **A meta-controller** decides in real time which branch should be driving 
  the signal — deferring to the RL policy when traffic is normal, and 
  escalating to the deliberative reasoning branch when the situation calls 
  for judgment rather than pattern-matching.

## Who This Is For and How It Helps

### City Traffic Authorities & Researchers
Explore next-generation adaptive signal control that doesn't trade safety for 
efficiency.

### Emergency Response Optimization
The system is built to detect and prioritize scenarios like emergency 
vehicles needing right-of-way, instead of treating every vehicle the same.

### Interpretable Traffic AI
Because the reasoning branch produces actual language explanations for its 
decisions rather than a black-box output, it's more auditable than a pure RL 
policy — which matters when city planners and regulators need to trust 
safety-critical infrastructure.

### Cross-City Generalization
The system has already been validated across genuinely different traffic 
environments (Hong Kong, France, South Korea), showing it isn't overfit to 
one city's driving patterns or road layout.

## In Short

VLMLight gives traffic signals the ability to act fast when conditions are 
normal, and stop to actually think when they're not — addressing the core 
blind spot of today's purely reactive, RL-based traffic control systems.

**Challenges we ran into**

### Environment & dependency hell on Windows
Getting the simulation + RL stack running locally was harder than expected. 
The project's dependencies (TransSimHub, which wraps SUMO for traffic 
simulation, plus PyTorch/RL libraries) assume a fairly standard Python setup — 
we were initially on Python 3.14, which is too new for several packages in 
the stack. Sub-dependencies like `tinyscaler` (used by the multi-agent RL 
wrapper `supersuit`) don't ship prebuilt wheels for 3.14, so pip tried to 
compile it from source — which then failed because the Windows build tools 
were missing the Windows SDK (`io.h` header not found).

**Fix:** Rebuilt the environment in a Python 3.11 virtual environment instead 
of fighting the 3.14 compatibility gap. That gave us prebuilt wheels for 
everything, no local compilation needed, and a clean, isolated dependency set.

### Flaky large-file downloads
One dependency, `sumo_data` (a ~130MB wheel bundling SUMO's simulation 
network data), kept timing out mid-download on a slower connection. 

**Fix:** Increased pip's default timeout and retry count 
(`--default-timeout=120 --retries 10`) rather than relying on pip's default 
15-second read timeout, which was too aggressive for the file size.

### Regional API access restrictions
The project's default LLM/VLM config points at Alibaba's DashScope API — 
but DashScope has stopped accepting new signups from India, which blocked 
us from using the intended hosted backend entirely.

**Fix:** Since the underlying models (Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL) are 
open and hosted by multiple providers, we swapped to an OpenAI-compatible 
provider (OpenRouter) that exposes the same models without geographic 
signup restrictions — a small config change since `qwen-agent` already 
supports generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints, not just DashScope.

### Local hardware constraints
The reference setup assumes self-hosting a 72B LLM and 32B VLM, which needs 
serious multi-GPU VRAM we don't have access to.

**Fix:** Used a hosted inference API instead of local serving, which let us 
run the full decision pipeline without needing a GPU cluster.

**Road Safety**

VLMLight fits strongly into the Road Safety domain because it is designed to make traffic signals respond not only to normal traffic conditions but also to potentially dangerous situations in real time. Traditional traffic signals generally follow fixed timings or fast reinforcement-learning decisions, but VLMLight adds an intelligent reasoning layer that can recognize safety-critical events such as an approaching ambulance, a pedestrian still crossing the road, an accident or blocked lane, and dangerous traffic congestion. For example, if an ambulance is approaching from the North, VLMLight can detect it through camera feeds, prioritize its movement, extend the appropriate green signal, and keep conflicting directions stopped so the emergency vehicle can pass safely. Similarly, when one road has a very long queue and high waiting time while another direction has very little traffic, the system can intelligently redistribute green time instead of giving equal time to both directions, reducing unnecessary waiting and the possibility of congestion and queue spillback. The system can also protect pedestrians by extending crossing time when necessary and prevent vehicles from entering a blocked or accident-affected lane. Therefore, VLMLight is not simply an intelligent traffic optimization system; its main purpose is risk-aware traffic management, where safety, emergency response, pedestrian protection, congestion prevention, and efficient traffic flow are considered together. In simple terms, traditional signals react to traffic, while VLMLight reacts to traffic risk, making it a strong fit for the Road Safety domain.

![Cryptography](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cryptography-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![WebSockets](https://img.shields.io/badge/WebSockets-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![UDP Socket](https://img.shields.io/badge/UDP%20Socket-333333?style=flat-square) ![FAST API](https://img.shields.io/badge/FAST%20API-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vite](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vite-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

VEIL-MESH addresses the problem of coordinating situational awareness and secure communications in contested or infrastructure-denied environments specifically:

- No reliable comms infrastructure  cell towers/satellite links can be jammed, destroyed, or simply absent (forward operating areas, disaster zones, remote perimeters). VEIL-MESH's answer: a zero-infrastructure, offline P2P encrypted mesh network where nodes relay messages directly, no base stations or internet required.

- Slow, manual threat detection  human operators can't watch every camera or sensor feed continuously. Its answer: edge AI (YOLOv8n for vision, Isolation Forest for telemetry anomalies) runs threat/anomaly detection locally on each node, generating alerts instead of raw data streams that need constant human review.

- Unsecured or unauthenticated field communications messages between distributed units/sensors are vulnerable to interception or spoofing. Its answer: encrypted, signed message envelopes with a per-node keyring, so every message is authenticated and confidential even without central infrastructure.

- Fragmented command visibility  no unified way to see what all distributed sensors/units are reporting. Its answer: a FastAPI bridge exposing alerts/messages/actions plus a WebSocket stream feeding a React operator console for real-time command visibility.

**Challenges we ran into**

- UDP packet loss/ordering — messages arriving out of order or dropped over the unreliable UDP mesh

- YOLO false positives — the vision sensor flagging non-threats as objects of interest

- Key exchange/sync issues across nodes — keeping the per-node keyring consistent as nodes join/relay

- WebSocket reconnect handling — keeping the operator console's real-time alert stream stable through disconnects

**Defence**

VEIL-MESH fits the Defence track because it's designed around core military operational problems, not generic tech:

1. Contested/denied environments
Military operations often happen where infrastructure is destroyed, jammed, or was never there forward operating bases, remote perimeters, disaster/conflict zones. VEIL-MESH's zero-infrastructure mesh means units can communicate securely without relying on cell towers, satellites, or fixed networks that an adversary could target or jam.

2. Secure tactical communications
Every message on the mesh is encrypted and signed with a per-node keyring meaning intercepted traffic can't be read, and spoofed/injected messages can't impersonate a real unit. This maps directly to military comms requirements: confidentiality + authentication in the field.

3. Situational awareness at the edge
YOLOv8n (vision) and Isolation Forest (telemetry anomaly detection) run locally on each node so threat/anomaly detection happens right where the sensor is, without needing to pipe raw video/data back to a command center over a vulnerable link. This gives forward units real-time awareness even when disconnected from higher command.

4. Command and control visibility
The FastAPI bridge + WebSocket stream + React console gives commanders a live operational picture of alerts, unit status, and actions a lightweight, deployable C2 (command and control) layer.

5. Autonomous, low-manpower monitoring
Edge AI acting as a "trigger engine" reduces the number of personnel needed to continuously monitor sensors/cameras relevant for perimeter security, remote outposts, or persistent surveillance where manning constraints matter.

### TraceTalk
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/tracetalk-8629) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Omkar-Ghongade/Push2Prod) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/oIdCc0ds9wQ) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Push%20to%20Prod%20Hackathon:%20Building%20at%20the%20Frontier-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://pushtoprod-india.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Can make distributed systems dashboard talk !

![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenObserve](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenObserve-333333?style=flat-square)

**How you are solving it?**

**TraceTalk** replaces query-builder UIs with conversation. An engineer asks a plain-language question ("why did payment latency spike at 2pm?") and an AI agent investigates live querying logs, metrics, and traces showing its reasoning trail alongside evidence-grounded answers.

## What We Built

1. **5 query tools** — `run_sql`, `list_streams`, `search_logs`, `get_metrics`, `get_service_graph` wrapping SQL queries against OpenObserve

2. **Claude agent loop** — Multi-step tool-use with streaming narration, evidence grounding, and 20-call budget cap

3. **SSE streaming backend** — Flask server streams investigation events in real-time via Server-Sent Events

4. **Interactive frontend** — Next.js chat interface with live investigation panel showing agent narrations and tool results as they happen

**How Did You Use Claude?**

- **Tool-use loop**: Claude decides which tools to call based on the user's question, chaining calls across services to trace root cause
- **System prompt engineering**: Custom prompt instructs Claude to act as an SRE, ground every claim in tool results, emit narrations for the UI, and cap investigation at 20 calls
- **Multi-hop reasoning**: Claude autonomously chains evidence e.g., metrics → service graph → logs → traces to answer ambiguous questions without being told which service or time window to investigate
- **Streaming narration**: Each Claude turn produces narrations ("Checking payment-service latency...") that stream to the UI in real-time, making the investigation visible

**What is the deployed URL for this project?**

https://github.com/Omkar-Ghongade/Push2Prod

**What is the problem your project solves?**

When something breaks in a distributed system, the person on call doesn't get a root cause they get a wall of dashboards. Debugging today means manually jumping between three or four disconnected tools a metrics dashboard for the symptom, a log search UI for the evidence, a tracing tool for the request path and hand-writing a different query language in each one, all while a service is actively degraded.

This has two costs:

Speed. Every minute spent translating "why is checkout slow" into the right PromQL query, then the right SPL query, then the right trace filter, is a minute the incident stays open.
Access. This workflow assumes deep, tool-specific expertise. An engineer who didn't build the system, or who's newer to on-call, often can't investigate as fast as the person who wrote the original queries so the same few people end up paged for everything.

TraceTalk removes the translation step. You ask what you actually want to know, in plain language "why did payment-service latency spike around 2pm?" and an agent investigates the way a senior engineer would: it queries the metrics, follows the evidence into the logs, checks the trace, and answers with the specific numbers and log lines that back up its conclusion. Nothing is asserted without a tool call behind it, and the side panel shows every step live, so the answer is verifiable, not just plausible.

The result isn't a smarter dashboard. It's a different way of interacting with observability data entirely closer to debugging with a colleague than querying a database.

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/quickavault-9e04) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/thecont1/Quick2AVault) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://flatwrite.md/?s=kO4go0VZ.md) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Push%20to%20Prod%20Hackathon:%20Building%20at%20the%20Frontier-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://pushtoprod-india.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Who's the boss of your money? Why, you are!

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Swift](https://img.shields.io/badge/Swift-333333?style=flat-square) ![Dart](https://img.shields.io/badge/Dart-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flutter](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flutter-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![AnyDoc](https://img.shields.io/badge/AnyDoc-333333?style=flat-square)

**What is the deployed URL for this project?**

Haha trick question, right? There is no public URL. Quick2AVault is local-first by design.

**How Did You Use Claude?**

Claude is the judgment layer, not a feature. Its only product is structured truth: strict tool-schema JSON extracted from canonical markdown (determinism via forced tool_choice — Claude 5 rejects the temperature parameter). Claude drives entity resolution (knowing a wallet-load is a transfer, not spending; that Swiggy the merchant, Swiggy the equity, and the Swiggy wallet are three different entities) and the reconciliation semantics that collapse duplicate evidence into one transaction.

The day's hardest bug was an AI-semantics bug — the extractor invented accounts and booked a salary as a transfer — fixed by bounding model authority with code invariants: a prompt is not an invariant. User-confirmed values are never overwritten by AI. And through the MCP adapter, Claude becomes an interface to the vault: ask "what did I spend this FY?" and get an answer with evidence links.

**How you are solving it?**

A headless TypeScript daemon runs a three-phase pipeline: SHA-256 intake with dedupe → deterministic markdown conversion → Claude extraction into a strict JSON schema. The canonical schema models any economic event — who paid whom, how much, why, when, how, with what evidence — using four entity kinds (person/organisation/account/instrument), double-entry transaction legs, and documents-as-evidence, with invariants enforced as database constraints (integer minor units; transfers structurally excluded from spending). A scored reconciliation engine links invoices to bank alerts: one rupee, counted once.

Three clients share one versioned Core API: a web UI, a native macOS menubar app, and an MCP server — so an AI agent can query your finances with full provenance. Jurisdiction packs (India + Japan shipped) make every country data, not code.

Proven on 69 real documents → 67 transactions, 0 failures — including catching a ₹1,68,641 salary misbooked as a transfer, and separating ₹2,05,943 of investments from honest spending of ₹40,283.

Disclosure: the repo root contains a pre-existing macOS prototype (Glaze runtime) and prior architecture plans. Everything under daemon/ and desktop/ — the daemon, schema, extraction, reconciliation, MCP server, both UIs, jurisdiction packs, Learning Mode — was built in the hackathon window on branch hack/push-to-prod.

**What is the problem your project solves?**

Personal finance software is built on a false premise: that your bank feed is the truth and your documents are clutter. The consequences are everywhere. A single credit-card purchase produces a merchant invoice AND a bank confirmation — and every tool counts that rupee twice. Apps silo themselves: one does bank accounts, another mutual funds, a third stocks, so none can tell you what you're actually worth. And the price of admission is standing access to your email and bank accounts.

Quick2AVault inverts the premise: personal finance is a document-reconciliation problem, not an aggregation problem. You feed it documents — a watched folder, an email dropbox, an API — and it builds a deduplicated, reconciled, evidence-backed ledger of your economic life. On your machine. No standing access to anything.

> The universal mark of truth for the internet.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![AI/ML](https://img.shields.io/badge/AI/ML-333333?style=flat-square)

**What is the deployed URL for this project?**

https://satyamark.vercel.app/

**What is the problem your project solves?**

> *"The most expensive thing in the world is trust. Cheap people can't afford it."*

Misinformation and deepfakes spread faster than truth. Current fact-checking is **slow, siloed, and disconnected** from where content is consumed. When platforms do moderate, they provide opaque, binary "False" labels without context. Furthermore, real-time verification (RAG, forensics) is too computationally expensive for individual platforms to build. 

**SatyaMark** is an open-source, platform-agnostic verification engine. Instead of forcing users to hunt for facts, we bring the facts to them. We offer a lightweight React SDK that allows *any* platform to embed real-time fact-checking and AI-media detection directly into their UI, transforming opaque moderation into transparent, **evidence-backed trust signals**.

**How Did You Use Claude?**

Claude serves as the core reasoning and natural language engine powering our text verification pipeline within SatyaMark. We specifically integrated Claude into our Python-based AI workers (orchestrated via LangGraph) to handle the complex, nuanced tasks that traditional rule-based systems fail at. 

Here is exactly how we utilized Claude in the project:

**1. Intelligent Claim Extraction:**
Social media posts are inherently messy, filled with slang, opinions, and multiple overlapping statements. We use Claude to ingest raw, multi-modal input (text and image context) and extract distinct, verifiable factual claims from the noise. It accurately separates subjective opinions from objective assertions that require fact-checking.

**2. Agentic Reasoning & Cross-Verification:**
Claude acts as the "brain" within our LangGraph agentic loop. Once a claim is extracted, Claude determines the best search queries to retrieve relevant information from external APIs and our internal RAG database. It then analyzes the retrieved sources, reasoning across multiple (sometimes conflicting) pieces of evidence to determine if a claim is mathematically verifiable, completely false, or requires more context.

**3. Generating Transparent Explanations:**
A simple "False" label isn't enough to build trust. We leverage Claude's exceptional natural language generation capabilities to synthesize the gathered evidence into clear, unbiased, and easy-to-understand explanations. Claude takes the raw data and formulates the "Why" behind the verdict, presenting the user with a transparent summary that directly cites the sources it used to make its decision.

**How you are solving it?**

We built **SatyaMark** as a highly-scalable "mark of truth" infrastructure for the internet:

#### 🧠 1. Multi-Modal AI Workers
Independent, asynchronous AI workers handle the heavy lifting:
* **Text:** LangGraph-powered NLP agents extract claims and cross-verify via RAG databases (FAISS).
* **Media:** A forensic pipeline detects deepfakes and manipulation in real-time.

#### ⚙️ 2. Asynchronous Orchestration
To prevent UI blocking, our Node.js Backend routes verification requests via **Redis Streams** and caches results in **PostgreSQL**. This decouples expensive AI inference from user interactions.

#### 🔌 3. The React SDK (`satyamark-react`)
Developers can drop our SDK into any app to instantly display verification icons. It connects via **WebSockets**, pushing live AI updates directly to the client.

#### 🔍 4. Radical Transparency
We don't just say "False." Clicking our icon reveals *why*: cited sources, confidence scores, and a manual recheck loop.

> Arbitrary-precision decimal arithmetic

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-333333?style=flat-square) ![WebAssembly](https://img.shields.io/badge/WebAssembly-333333?style=flat-square) ![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-333333?style=flat-square) ![Golang](https://img.shields.io/badge/Golang-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

# The Problem decimal-go Solves

## The float64 problem

Computers that use IEEE-754 `float64` (every mainstream language's default)
cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly:

```go
0.1 + 0.2 // = 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3
19.99 * 3 // = 59.96999999999999, not 59.97
```

These tiny errors compound. Money, rates, taxes, measurements, and financial
calculations cannot be done safely in `float64` — at some point a penny is
lost, a total is off, or a comparison fails (`0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `false`).

## The existing solutions (and their gaps)

- **JavaScript** has `decimal.js` — the de-facto standard arbitrary-precision
  decimal library (10k+ stars, used across the industry). It is exact,
  battle-tested, and its API is widely known.
- **Go** had **no drop-in behavioral equivalent**. Alternatives like
  `shopspring/decimal` are popular but differ in construction, rounding, and
  formatting semantics. Code migrated from JS to Go cannot compile against
  them "as-is", and subtle rounding differences silently change results.

## What decimal-go does

decimal-go is a **behavioral port of decimal.js v10.6.0 to Go**:

- **Exact**: arbitrary-precision decimal arithmetic on base-1e7 coefficient
  words — no float rounding at any step (except the transcendental ops, which
  round to the constructor's precision exactly like the original).
- **Same semantics as the reference**: every construction rule, rounding
  mode, edge case (NaN, ±Infinity, ±0, hex/bin/oct literals), formatting
  rule, and the 42 long-form aliases (`DividedBy`, `NaturalLogarithm`, …) —
  verified **byte-for-byte** against the live decimal.js (1518 cross-validated
  cases) plus all 61 original test modules.
- **Idiomatic Go**: short names (`Div`, `Sqrt`, `Ln`), immutable values,
  `encoding.TextMarshaler` / JSON / `database/sql` integration, per-context
  constructors for safe concurrency (race-free by design — the JS module-level
  flags were moved onto the constructor).
- **Zero dependencies** — the standard library only.

## Who needs it

- Go services that handle money, invoicing, banking, e-commerce totals.
- Ports of existing JS financial codebases (decimal.js API is preserved).
- Any Go application needing reproducible, exactly-rounded decimals at any
  precision (e.g. 1000-digit division) with no float surprises.

## One-line summary

> Go needed exact, decimal.js-compatible decimal arithmetic; float64 can't
> do it, and existing Go libraries don't match decimal.js behavior —
> decimal-go brings the reference behavior, verified byte-for-byte, to Go.

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges We Ran Into

## 1. Faithful porting of decimal.js internals

decimal.js is optimized JS: 14-digit floating-point chunks (`0.5 * 1e14`),
`Math`-based guards, bit-twiddling for exponent bounds, and a hand-written
parser. Porting to Go meant re-deriving every algorithm on `int32` base-1e7
words — while keeping **identical** results, not just similar ones.

**Fix**: white-box porting — ran the original's own test suite (61 modules)
against the Go package, in the same order, plus a cross-validation harness
(`xvalidate/`, 1518 cases) that diffs Go output against live Node decimal.js.

## 2. Three real bugs found the hard way

Regression tests lock these in:

- **pow10 overflow**: the power-of-ten table indexed out of range at extreme
  exponents.
- **Pow with negative exponent**: an index error when the exponent is
  negative (porting `abs(n)` + `isNeg(n)` orderings from the JS).
- **`1^±Infinity`**: the identity case produced the wrong value.

**Lesson**: a port is only as good as its edge-case coverage — parity tests
are the product, not a nicety.

## 3. The OOM/hang in fuzzing (CI "hung" failure)

`FuzzArith` "hung" in CI. Diagnosis showed it was not a hang but a memory
blowup: `Mod`/`Divide` materialize the quotient digit-by-digit — with inputs
like `0b1p2738415519256` (a binary literal with an astronomically large
exponent) the quotient would be ~10^824 *billion* digits. The reference
decimal.js **hangs identically** (node exits by timeout).

**Fix**: documented in `docs/DECISIONS.md` §7 — the library stays uncapped
(parity), the fuzz harness is bounded (`maxQuotientWords = 1e5` guard skips
quotients too large to be meaningful).

## 4. Concurrency: decimal.js global mutable state

decimal.js uses module-level mutable flags (`external`, `inexact`,
`quadrant`). That is a data race when shared across goroutines.

**Fix**: moved those flags onto the `Constructor` — one clone per concurrent
context, `go test -race` clean. This is a semantic change we made deliberately
and documented, because Go code is expected to run concurrently.

## 5. Honest benchmarking

Marketing-wise it's tempting to cherry-pick. The reality: 18/20 directly
comparable op pairs are faster in Go, but string parsing is ~1.45× slower
(V8's JIT excels at it) — so parse→op→format round trips are ~1.7× slower.

**Fix**: publish the full table with methodology (`bench/README.md`,
`bench/results.txt`) and disclose the slower paths instead of hiding them.

## 6. The WASM playground

Compiling the library to WebAssembly for the browser hit API quirks:
`log10` only exists as a constructor method (`decimal.Default.Log10`), not on
instances; `ToExponential`/`ToPrecision`/hex/bin/oct formatting return
`string` (not `Decimal`); there is no instance `IsInf` (use `!IsFinite`).
Also: the first commit accidentally included a stray 3.7 MB `playground`
binary — removed in a follow-up, and the build is now tagged
`//go:build js && wasm` so `go test ./...` never touches it.

## 7. Infra fiddliness (the unglamorous part)

- GitHub Pages was redirecting everything to a stale account-level custom
  domain (`sundram.me`, NXDOMAIN) — cleared via the Pages API.
- A fine-grained PAT couldn't push to the org Pages repo; a classic PAT with
  `repo` scope works (stored as a repo secret, used only by the sync
  workflow).
- Auto-updating `CHANGELOG.md` from draft-release bodies needed an idempotent
  script (else every push re-triggered itself into an infinite loop), plus
  handling release-drafter's "* No changes" empty filler.

> Migrate smarter. Validate everything

![Git](https://img.shields.io/badge/Git-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![Google API](https://img.shields.io/badge/Google%20API-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML/CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML/CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Modern software projects often need to be migrated from one programming language to another for better performance, maintainability, compatibility, or platform support. However, manually porting an entire codebase is time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to validate.

Our project addresses this problem by providing an AI-assisted cross-language code migration and validation platform. It analyzes an existing repository, assists with translating its functionality into another language, and then validates the migrated implementation through differential testing, fuzz testing, benchmarking, and automated debugging.

This helps developers migrate legacy or language-specific codebases more efficiently while ensuring that the new implementation maintains the behavior and correctness of the original code.

**Challenges we ran into**

Cross-language compatibility: Preserving the exact behavior of the original Python implementation while migrating it to Rust was challenging, especially for Unicode, emoji, terminal escape sequences, and edge cases.
Behavioral validation: A successful compilation does not guarantee that a migrated implementation behaves identically. We had to design differential testing to compare the original and migrated implementations across the same inputs.
Fuzz testing: Generating large numbers of meaningful edge-case inputs and identifying discrepancies between implementations required careful test design.
Repository complexity: Understanding dependencies, project structure, configuration files, and test suites from an existing repository added significant complexity to the migration process.
Build artifacts and environment differences: Managing Python and Rust environments, dependencies, compiled artifacts, and reproducible builds was another challenge.
AI-assisted debugging: Using AI to assist with migration and debugging required careful validation because generated code can introduce subtle behavioral differences that are difficult to detect without automated testing.
Time constraints: Building the migration pipeline, testing system, benchmarking tools, debugging workflow, and user interface within the hackathon time limit required prioritizing the most important features.

Team **Akash and co** -- Akashsaihari Sata, Ayesha Afreen, Lakshmi Prasanna, Athmaj Kalangi

> Building price-parser with 100% Behavioral Parity

![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges We Ran Into

## 1. Our test data had errors at first
A mismatch that looked like a Rust bug turned out to be a broken test‑data exporter. It included an option that wasn't actually passed to the Python parser. We fixed the exporter and regenerated the corpus — lesson learned: test your test tools.

## 2. Decimals didn't compare the same way
Python treats `644` and `644.0` as equal, but a simple string comparison would call them different. We changed the comparison to check the actual decimal values instead of raw strings or floats.

## 3. Rust's regex doesn't support Python's advanced features
The original code used look‑around and conditional patterns that Rust's `regex` crate doesn't have. Instead of adding a heavier engine, we rewrote those parts with ordinary Rust logic — keeping things fast and dependency‑light.

## 4. Unicode length is counted differently
Python counts characters; Rust counts bytes. For some currency symbols, those counts differ. We used character‑based counting wherever we needed to match Python's behaviour.

## 5. Benchmark results were inconsistent
Some runs made Rust look slower, others faster — depending on machine load. So we didn't claim a universal speedup. Instead, we used the benchmarks to find where time actually goes.

## 6. The real bottleneck was surprising
We thought the custom logic replacing regex would be slow, but the biggest drag was currency lookup — especially when the parser had to scan many currencies and fail to find a match early. That gave us a clear target for future improvements.

## 7. Fuzzing needs nightly Rust, but normal users shouldn't
`cargo-fuzz` requires a nightly toolchain, so we isolated it in a separate `fuzz/` package. The main crate stays on stable Rust 1.96.0.

## 8. GitHub didn't show the release workflow at first
The workflow file was pushed, but GitHub ignored it until we changed the trigger from `workflow_dispatch:` to `workflow_dispatch: {}` — then it appeared.

## 9. We had to handle licensing carefully
Since this project is based on an existing open‑source project, we preserved the original BSD‑3‑Clause license and copyright notices, adding our own files without claiming ownership or endorsement.

## 10. Publishing to crates.io had a couple of hiccups
The first attempt failed because our email wasn't verified. After verifying, it worked. We also accidentally exposed an API token during the process, revoked it immediately, and replaced it — a good reminder to handle credentials carefully.

**The problem it solves**

# Problems This Project Solves

## 1. Prices come in all shapes and sizes
Online prices are messy: `$12.99`, `205,68 €`, `CHF 1'049,95`, `USD 1,144.00`, `1.144.000`, `.75`, or even `Free`. This parser handles them all — figuring out the amount, currency, and original text no matter how they're written.

## 2. No behavior drift when switching from Python to Rust
A rewrite that *looks* right isn't good enough — it has to act right. We ran 1,057 real-world test cases through both the original Python and new Rust versions. Result: Rust passed every single one with zero mismatches in amounts, currencies, text representations, or missing values.

## 3. Exact money, no rounding errors
Using floating-point numbers for currency is a recipe for tiny, silent errors. This implementation uses exact decimal math (`rust_decimal::Decimal`), so even weird values like `1.11000000000000009770` stay perfectly precise.

## 4. Future changes are automatically safeguarded
The project runs automated checks on every update — building, testing, verifying test data, and re-running the Python/Rust comparison. If a change ever breaks the original behavior, we catch it immediately.

## 5. Tested against the weirdest possible inputs
Hand-written tests can't cover everything. So we also threw random text, odd Unicode, and automated fuzzing at the parser to uncover hidden crashes or edge cases that normal examples would miss.

## 6. Ready for other developers to use
This isn't just an internal script. It's a published Rust crate on [crates.io](https://crates.io) with a public GitHub repo, full docs, examples, benchmarks, CI, and a verified release process — so anyone can drop it into their own projects.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building a reliable agentic shopping workflow was the biggest challenge. Coordinating multiple merchant searches, ranking products, presenting results in a clean and intuitive interface, and maintaining a smooth end-to-end user experience required several design iterations.

Another major challenge was integrating the Prava Agentic Payments Sandbox. While implementing the complete checkout flow, I encountered an authentication issue during Visa passkey enrollment, where passkey creation consistently failed despite Windows Hello being enabled and testing across multiple browsers. I worked around this by isolating the payment flow, documenting the issue, and continuing development on the core shopping experience while coordinating with the platform team.

Balancing autonomous AI behavior with user control was also challenging. I refined the workflow so the AI performs the research and comparison, while the user always remains in control of the final purchase decision.

**The problem it solves**

Online shopping hasn't evolved for the AI era. Finding the right product still means opening multiple websites, comparing prices, reading reviews, checking seller credibility, and repeating the same process for every purchase.

Aria replaces this fragmented workflow with an autonomous shopping agent. Instead of manually browsing dozens of products, users simply describe what they want. Aria researches multiple merchants, evaluates products using real reviews and trusted signals, compares the best options, and completes the purchase through agentic payments once the user approves.

The result is a shopping experience where AI does the research, comparison, and execution—while the user only makes the crucial decision.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

Our project enhances Visa Intelligent Commerce by enabling AI agents to complete secure, passwordless purchases using Visa Payment Passkeys. By combining autonomous shopping with biometric authentication, we deliver faster checkouts, stronger fraud protection, and a seamless payment experience while keeping users in full control of transaction approval.

**OpenAI**

Our project leverages OpenAI models to power an intelligent shopping agent that understands natural language, recommends products, compares options, and autonomously assists users through checkout. By combining advanced reasoning with secure Visa payment passkeys, we deliver a seamless, conversational, and trustworthy commerce experience.

**Best Agentic User Experience**

Aria is designed around a human-first agentic experience. Instead of overwhelming users with endless product listings, it transparently shows the AI's reasoning, researches multiple merchants in real time, summarizes insights, and presents only the best recommendations. The user stays in control by approving the final purchase, creating an experience that is fast, intuitive, trustworthy, and effortless.

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

Aria is built specifically for agentic commerce. Instead of acting as a traditional search engine, it autonomously researches products across multiple merchants, compares prices and reviews, identifies the best option, and streamlines checkout through agentic payments while keeping the user in control of the final purchase decision. It demonstrates how AI agents can move beyond recommendations to execute real-world commerce workflows end-to-end.

### steward
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/steward-ad2f) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Pawansingh3889/steward) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Agentic%20Commerce%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://agentic-commerce.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> An agent that spends someone else's money well.

![SQLite](https://img.shields.io/badge/SQLite-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenAi](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenAi-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ollama](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ollama-333333?style=flat-square) ![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-333333?style=flat-square) ![Starlette](https://img.shields.io/badge/Starlette-333333?style=flat-square) ![prava](https://img.shields.io/badge/prava-333333?style=flat-square) ![Linq](https://img.shields.io/badge/Linq-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

**The Linq adapter I wrote from the docs was wrong in every particular,** and I only found out by sending one message to a real handset. It is not `POST /messages` with to/from/body — it is `POST /chats/{chat_id}/messages` with `{"message": {"parts": [{"type":"text","value":...}]}}`. Messages address a *chat*, not a number, and the chat carries the protocol — hence iMessage.

**`get_audit_log` had never once returned a row, at any size.** Found when a ledger panel came back empty for a household that had just made two attempts. FastMCP emits one content block per list item and my code joined them before parsing: 0 rows read as "no reply", so an empty log looked like a dead engine; 1 row decoded to a bare dict the caller discarded for not being a list; 2 rows became `{...}{...}`, not JSON. Three sizes, three silent wrong answers.

**The daily budget can be beaten by waiting.** Approving a parked purchase never re-checks the budget and the row keeps its timestamp, so an approval at 23:00 lands on a day that may already be spent. Found by a simulator that replays the real engine at synthetic timestamps, so it reproduced the hole instead of hiding it.

**There was no way for a person to say no.** Refusing left the row identical to one nobody had read yet, so the spender was never told and no approval rate had an honest denominator. I added a `rejected` verdict and a `reject_purchase` tool, kept distinct from a policy denial: a rule refusing and a parent refusing are different sentences. Timing each answer showed something I would not have guessed: on a month of simulated traffic, people take about six times longer to say no than yes.

**A test failed on my own fixtures, correctly.** Every offer shown must be cheaper, or faster, or both. One supplier was cheapest *and* fastest for soap, leaving the person no decision, so I rebuilt the catalogue.

*Three of the above are in pay-warden, which predates the event. The code is prior work; finding and fixing these was not.*

**The problem it solves**

Most agentic-commerce demos have an agent buy something for the person who owns the card. I can buy my own socks, so the agent is a novelty there.

The real need is when the spender and payer are different people, and the payer can't approve every purchase: a student on an allowance, a parent whose adult child manages their money.

## The Solution

The spender texts what they need. steward finds options, and every spend goes through pay-warden — a separate process holding the Prava credentials and evaluating a YAML policy the sponsor wrote.

Under the limit, it goes through. Over it, the purchase parks and the sponsor gets a text with the exact rule that fired. The sponsor sees decisions, the ledger, and escalations — never the conversation, unless the spender shares a turn.

## Why It Works Today

The hard part isn't buying — it's permission. Anyone handing someone else money already does this badly over WhatsApp.

## Real Merchants

I graded 23 merchants for agent-readiness. The best scored a B, and the big general stores that would actually sell soap topped out at C. So the catalogue stays modelled and says FIXTURE on every screen until that changes.

---

**Disclosure:** the starting point was three of my own earlier projects — payoptimize's LLM wrapper and redactor, pay-warden's policy engine and Prava rail, and canibuy's merchant grading. Built this weekend: the two-line spender/sponsor flow, savings plans, the Linq iMessage integration, the pilot event log, and the sponsor dashboard.

**The problem it solves**

The Problem It Solves

Earthquakes happen without warning and can cause serious damage, injuries, and loss of life. Many people do not receive timely information about nearby earthquakes, understand the risks, or know what actions to take before, during, and after an earthquake.

Traditional earthquake information is often scattered across multiple websites, difficult to understand, or delayed, making it harder for people to stay informed and prepared.

How RAA Earthquake Helps

RAA Earthquake is a real-time earthquake monitoring and alert platform designed to make earthquake information accessible, easy to understand, and actionable for everyone.

Key Uses
 Monitor Earthquakes Worldwide
View recent earthquakes from around the world in real time.
Track magnitude, depth, location, and time of occurrence.
 Location-Based Awareness
Stay informed about earthquakes occurring near your region.
Understand potential risks based on proximity and earthquake intensity.
 Interactive Earthquake Map
Visualize earthquake activity on an interactive global map.
Quickly identify earthquake hotspots and affected regions.
 Real-Time Alerts
Receive updates about significant seismic events as they happen.
Reduce the time needed to discover important earthquake information.
 Historical Analysis
Explore earthquake activity over the last 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days.
Identify patterns and trends in seismic activity.
Earthquake Safety Education
Learn what to do before, during, and after an earthquake.
Access preparedness guides and safety resources.
 Community Awareness
Share and view earthquake experiences through community feedback features.
Help others understand real-world impacts in affected areas.
Benefits
For Individuals
Stay informed about nearby earthquakes.
Improve personal and family preparedness.
Access reliable earthquake information quickly.
For Students & Researchers
Study seismic activity through real-world data.
Analyze earthquake patterns and geographic trends.
For Travelers
Monitor earthquake activity in destinations before and during travel.
Stay aware of potential natural hazards.
For Communities
Increase public awareness of earthquake risks.
Encourage better emergency preparedness and disaster response.
Why RAA Earthquake is Different

RAA Earthquake combines real-time monitoring, interactive visualization, safety education, and location-based awareness in a single platform, making earthquake information easier to access, understand, and act upon.

Its goal is to help people stay informed, prepared, and safer in the face of seismic events around the world.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building RAA Earthquake involved several technical and operational challenges. One of the biggest difficulties was creating a system that could provide real-time earthquake data while remaining fast, reliable, and easy to use.

1. Real-Time Data Integration

One challenge was fetching and displaying earthquake information from external data sources in real time. APIs occasionally returned incomplete data, different data formats, or temporary connection errors.

How I solved it:

Implemented error handling and validation checks.
Added automatic data refresh mechanisms.
Created fallback logic to prevent the application from breaking when data was temporarily unavailable.
2. Interactive Global Map Performance

Displaying hundreds of earthquake markers on a live map affected performance, especially on slower devices.

How I solved it:

Optimized marker rendering.
Reduced unnecessary map updates.
Improved data loading efficiency so users could view earthquake information smoothly.
3. Accurate Location Display

Converting earthquake coordinates into understandable locations for users was challenging because many earthquakes occur in remote areas.

How I solved it:

Integrated reverse geocoding services.
Added location processing logic to generate more user-friendly place names.
4. Website Reliability and Uptime

During development, the application occasionally became unavailable due to hosting limitations and deployment issues.

How I solved it:

Improved deployment configuration.
Optimized server settings and monitoring.
Implemented reliability improvements to keep the platform accessible and responsive.
5. User Experience and Accessibility

Presenting large amounts of seismic data without overwhelming users was difficult.

How I solved it:

Redesigned the interface multiple times.
Added visual indicators for magnitude and depth.
Created a clean dashboard and interactive map for easier navigation.
6. SEO and Discoverability

Ensuring that people could find earthquake information through search engines required additional optimization.

How I solved it:

Improved page structure and metadata.
Added educational content and safety guides.
Optimized loading speed and mobile responsiveness.
What I Learned

This project taught me how to work with real-time data, handle API failures, optimize performance, improve deployment reliability, and design user-friendly interfaces. It also helped me better understand the importance of building systems that remain useful and reliable during critical situations when users need information the most.

> "Hiring Smarter, Ranking Better."

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![AI/ML](https://img.shields.io/badge/AI/ML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/React.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vite](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vite-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hybrid Scoring Mechanism](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hybrid%20Scoring%20Mechanism-333333?style=flat-square) ![Dataset-driven Testing & Validation](https://img.shields.io/badge/Dataset--driven%20Testing%20&%20Validation-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Problem Statement
RecruitIQ – AI-Powered Candidate Ranking System

Traditional Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) rely heavily on keyword matching, often overlooking highly qualified candidates whose experience and potential do not exactly mirror the wording of a job description. As a result, recruiters spend significant time manually reviewing applications and may still miss the best-fit talent.

RecruitIQ addresses this challenge by building an AI-driven candidate ranking system that evaluates applicants the way an experienced recruiter would. Instead of simply matching keywords, the system understands the context and intent behind job requirements and candidate profiles.

The solution:

Analyzes job descriptions to understand the actual needs of the role.
Evaluates candidates using a holistic approach, including career history, skills, experience patterns, and behavioral indicators.
Uses semantic understanding to identify candidates who genuinely fit the position, even when exact keywords are absent.
Produces a ranked shortlist that recruiters can trust, reducing screening time while improving hiring quality.

The goal is to bridge the gap between automated filtering and human judgment by enabling smarter, fairer, and more efficient recruitment decisions.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges I Ran Into
Semantic Matching vs Keyword Matching

One of the biggest hurdles was ensuring that the system could recognize relevant candidates even when they used different terminology than the job description.

For example, a candidate might mention:

"Built responsive user interfaces using component-based architecture"

while the job description explicitly asks for:

"React.js Frontend Development"

A basic keyword-based approach would score this candidate poorly despite having relevant experience.

How I Solved It
I shifted from relying solely on direct keyword comparisons to a semantic understanding approach.
Candidate profiles and job descriptions were processed into structured representations before scoring.
Multiple factors such as skills, experience relevance, and contextual similarity were combined to generate the final ranking.
I also experimented with different scoring weights and validation using sample datasets to improve the quality of recommendations.

This significantly improved the relevance of shortlisted candidates and reduced false negatives caused by wording differences.

Specific Bug/Hurdle
Inconsistent Candidate Ranking

During development, I noticed that candidates with strong overall profiles were sometimes ranked below less suitable candidates because one scoring component dominated the final score.

For example, candidates with many matching skills but limited relevant experience occasionally outranked more experienced applicants.

Resolution

I redesigned the ranking logic to use a hybrid weighted scoring mechanism, where different aspects contributed proportionally to the final score:

Skill relevance
Experience alignment
Career trajectory
Contextual similarity
Additional candidate indicators

After calibrating these weights using the provided datasets and repeated testing, the rankings became more stable and aligned much better with recruiter expectations.

Aditya Mittal

### SMART COMPLAINT REGISTRATION SYSTEM
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/smart-complaint-registration-system-ecf6) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-CodeStorm%202026%20#2-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://codestorm-week2-2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Campus complaints, tracked end to end

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![MySQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/MySQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![XAMPP](https://img.shields.io/badge/XAMPP-333333?style=flat-square) ![phpMyAdmin](https://img.shields.io/badge/phpMyAdmin-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

The main challenge was designing a workflow that matches how complaints actually move inside an institution. A complaint can begin with a student, be reviewed by a mentor, escalated to the HOD, sent to the principal, and finally marked as resolved. To support this, the database needed fields for complaint code, status, priority, assigned role, anonymity, uploaded files, and timestamps.

Another challenge was keeping the system useful for different types of users. Students need a simple form and tracking page, while administrators need dashboards with totals, priority indicators, and actions such as view, resolve, and forward. We solved this by separating the student-facing flow from the admin routes and making each role dashboard show only the complaints relevant to that authority.

The project also required practical backend handling: generating unique complaint codes, saving uploaded files safely, connecting Flask with MySQL, configuring the database through phpMyAdmin/XAMPP, and sending email updates through SMTP. These details helped turn the project from a basic form into a more complete complaint management system.

A final challenge was presenting the system clearly. The UI was kept minimal and direct: students see submission and tracking screens, while admins see tables, priority levels, complaint details, and action links. This keeps the workflow understandable even for non-technical campus users.

**The problem it solves**

Smart Complaint Registration System is a Flask-based campus grievance platform that turns informal complaint handling into a traceable digital workflow. Instead of students reporting issues verbally or through scattered messages, the system gives them a single place to submit complaints, attach proof, receive a unique tracking code, and follow the status of their complaint.

**What it does**

- Lets students submit complaints by category, title, description, email, and optional file attachment.
- Supports anonymous complaint submission when students do not want their name shown.
- Generates a unique complaint code for every submission so students can track progress later.
- Provides tracking pages where students can view complaint status, priority, category, and submitted date.
- Includes role-based dashboards for Mentor, HOD, and Principal users.
- Allows complaints to be reviewed, prioritized, forwarded, and resolved through the correct authority level.
- Sends email notifications for key complaint actions such as registration, forwarding, and resolution.

**How it is built**

The backend is written in Python using Flask. MySQL stores complaint records, admin users, status values, priorities, assignment levels, timestamps, and uploaded file references. The database is managed through phpMyAdmin and run locally with XAMPP. The frontend uses HTML and CSS templates to keep the student pages and admin dashboards simple, readable, and fast.

**Why it matters**

For students, the project creates confidence because every complaint gets a code and visible status. For staff, it creates a structured queue instead of scattered requests. For management, it gives a clear escalation path from Mentor to HOD to Principal, helping institutions handle academic, hostel, infrastructure, and other complaints more responsibly.

> Smarter Traffic Safer City

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Framer](https://img.shields.io/badge/Framer-333333?style=flat-square) ![Charts.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Charts.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML5​](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML5​-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Problem Statement

Modern urban traffic management systems struggle to cope with the rapidly changing conditions of today's cities. Most traffic intersections continue to operate using predefined or fixed-time signal schedules, which are unable to adapt dynamically to fluctuations in vehicle density, road incidents, weather conditions, or emergency situations. As a result, congestion continues to increase, causing longer travel times, excessive fuel consumption, higher carbon emissions, and significant economic losses.

One of the most critical challenges is the movement of emergency vehicles such as ambulances, fire trucks, and police vehicles. In conventional traffic systems, these vehicles are often forced to wait at congested intersections because traffic signals operate independently and lack real-time coordination. Even delays of a few minutes can have serious consequences in medical emergencies and disaster response.

Another major limitation is the lack of real-time situational awareness. Traffic operators typically monitor multiple CCTV feeds simultaneously, making it difficult to detect congestion, identify incidents, or respond quickly to changing road conditions. Existing systems rarely provide predictive insights or intelligent recommendations, forcing operators to make decisions manually under time pressure.

Furthermore, current traffic management platforms often function as isolated systems rather than integrated decision-support platforms. They provide raw monitoring data but do not explain why congestion is occurring, how it will evolve, or what actions should be taken. This lack of explainability reduces trust in automation and limits operational efficiency.

As cities continue to expand and vehicle volumes increase, there is an urgent need for a traffic management platform that can:

Analyze live traffic conditions in real time using AI and computer vision. 

Dynamically optimize traffic signal timings based on actual road conditions rather than fixed schedules.
Prioritize emergency vehicles by creating coordinated green corridors across multiple intersections.
Predict congestion before it becomes critical instead of reacting after delays occur.
Provide traffic operators with explainable AI recommendations that support faster and more informed decision-making.
Offer a real-time digital representation of the city, allowing operators to visualize traffic flow, monitor system health, and interact with the network through an intuitive command center.

Without intelligent, adaptive traffic management, cities will continue to experience increasing congestion, delayed emergency response, inefficient road utilization, higher environmental impact, and reduced quality of urban mobility.

FlowPulse AI addresses these challenges by bringing together computer vision, adaptive traffic signal optimization, a real-time Smart City Digital Twin, predictive analytics, and an AI-powered traffic operations copilot into a unified web-based platform. Rather than simply monitoring traffic, the platform continuously analyzes road conditions, explains AI-driven decisions, recommends optimal actions, coordinates emergency vehicle movement, and enables operators to manage complex urban traffic networks more efficiently through a modern, interactive command center.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges We Ran Into

Developing FlowPulse AI required combining several complex technologies—including computer vision, real-time simulation, AI-assisted decision support, and an interactive web application—into a single cohesive platform. Throughout development, we encountered a number of technical and design challenges.

1. Real-Time Video Processing

Running object detection on live or uploaded traffic videos while maintaining a smooth user experience was one of our biggest challenges. Computer vision inference is computationally expensive, and processing every frame significantly reduced playback performance. We optimized the processing pipeline by separating video rendering from AI inference and minimizing unnecessary UI updates.

2. Building a Realistic Digital Twin

Creating an interactive Smart City Digital Twin that accurately represents intersections, traffic flow, and congestion required careful planning. We needed to ensure that vehicles, traffic signals, and road states remained synchronized while keeping the interface responsive and intuitive.

3. Emergency Vehicle Coordination

Designing the emergency green corridor logic was more challenging than simply detecting an ambulance. The system had to identify the optimal route, coordinate multiple intersections, dynamically adjust signal phases, and restore normal traffic flow once the emergency vehicle had passed—all while making these decisions visually understandable.

4. AI Explainability

Instead of integrating AI as a generic chatbot, we wanted it to function as an intelligent traffic operations assistant. Designing Gemini to explain optimization decisions, justify recommendations, and summarize traffic conditions in a way that operators could quickly understand required careful prompt engineering and contextual data integration.

5. Performance Optimization

The application combines multiple real-time components, including a Digital Twin, animated dashboards, live analytics, and AI updates. Maintaining smooth performance while preventing unnecessary re-renders and ensuring a responsive user interface required continuous optimization throughout development.

6. Balancing Complexity and Usability

Traffic management systems can quickly become overwhelming due to the amount of information they present. One of our biggest design challenges was simplifying complex traffic analytics into a clean, intuitive interface without sacrificing important operational insights.

7. Creating a Hackathon-Ready Experience

Beyond functionality, we focused on delivering an engaging user experience. Building an interactive demo, integrating real-time AI insights, and ensuring every feature worked together seamlessly required multiple design iterations and extensive testing.

This project challenged us not only to solve technical problems but also to think like traffic engineers, AI developers, and product designers simultaneously. It reinforced the importance of balancing performance, usability, scalability, and explainable AI when building intelligent systems for real-world smart city applications
